chapters.title: What to Do in N.Y.C. This Winter
chapters.subtitle: You’re reading the Goings On newsletter, a guide to what we’re watching, listening to, and doing. Sign up to receive it in your in-box.

paragraphs.text: The holiday blitz seems to be creeping up earlier every year—and there’s plenty of cheer to go around at venues across the city in the next couple of months. (We see you, “A Kidman Carol.”) But winter is also a time to settle in for serious entertainment. Big theatre stars mix with big movie stars on the boards—including Adrienne Warren in a reimagining of Douglas Sirk’s “Imitation of Life,” from Lynn Nottage and John Legend, plus Paul Rudd and Julia Roberts in a gem of a play by Bess Wohl (“Liberation”). In the art world, the eternal, ever-new project of rethinking the past continues with an exhibition at the Met which considers the vast influences on ancient Greek art; New York City Ballet brings us a fresh look at Shakespeare’s most tragic romance. Stevie Wonder graces us with a performance of the still ground-shaking sounds of his landmark album from 1976. Claire Chase has a new installment of her quarter-century-long flute project.

paragraphs.text: The movie studios save many of what they believe to be their most Oscar-worthy films for a late-year release, and this time the lineup shimmers with what promise to be riveting turns from Julianne Moore, Miles Teller, and Andrew Scott—and perhaps even from Brad Pitt, in a reunion with the director David Fincher, for a sequel, on IMAX only (at least at first), to Quentin Tarantino’s “Once Upon a Time . . . in Hollywood.” If all you really want is to curl up under a weighted blanket at home, there’s plenty to catch on the small screen, too, including an ambitious William Gibson adaptation, a return of the “Parks and Recreation” duo Mike Schur and Amy Poehler, and a new rom-com starring Ayo Edebiri, some very good excuses to hibernate.—Shauna Lyon

paragraphs.text: Tech billionaires are inescapable this season, as the backlash against Silicon Valley gains momentum not only in our politics but in our entertainment. The documentary “Elon,” the Sam Altman bio-pic “Artificial,” and the Facebook feature “The Social Reckoning” spotlight the bros, while the Elizabeth Holmes-centered “You Can See Every-thing” and the crypto-focussed “The Altruists” (Nov. 19) take on the bilkers. In the latter, Anthony Boyle and Julia Garner star as Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison, the romantically linked execs whose mismanagement of funds at the crypto exchange FTX led to an eight-billion-dollar hole in the company’s balance sheet.

paragraphs.text: Audiences seeking a more traditional love story will find it in the latest page-to-screen rendering of “Pride and Prejudice” (Dec. 3), one of several literary adaptations to début this winter. The Jane Austen drama, a six-part miniseries on Netflix, features Emma Corrin and Jack Lowden as pop culture’s most beloved enemies to lovers, and Olivia Colman as the silly Mrs. Bennet. Rose Byrne and Meghann Fahy star as two estranged sisters forced to revisit a violent turning point in their childhoods in Peacock’s “The Good Daughter” (Nov. 12), based on the novel by Karin Slaughter. Controversy is already dogging “Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone” (Dec. 25), HBO’s TV reboot of the Hogwarts franchise.

paragraphs.text: There are also less conventional picks for series adaptation. Jhumpa Lahiri’s best-selling short-story collection “Unaccustomed Earth” (Dec. 17), about first- and second-generation Indian Americans navigating cross-cultural dynamics, is the unlikely source material for a Netflix series. William Gibson’s landmark cyberpunk novel “Neuromancer,” from 1984—long considered “unfilmable” because of its virtual setting and its fragmented narration—will get its first screen adaptation (Jan. 22). Callum Turner stars in the dystopian Apple TV thriller as a traumatized superhacker named Case who partners with an assassin, played by Briana Middleton, to steal from a corporate dynasty; the title refers to an artificial intelligence that threatens to indefinitely trap Case in a comforting simulation.

paragraphs.text: Finally, in a comedy-starved television landscape, lighter fare offers some warmth in the coming months. More than a decade after the end of “Parks and Recreation,” Amy Poehler returns with “Dig” (Nov. 23), a Peacock sitcom about a team of archeologists in Greece whose latest discovery sets off a far-reaching plot; co-created by the “Parks” showrunner Mike Schur, it co-stars Hugh Laurie and Geraldine Viswanathan. A different set of brainiacs get themselves into trouble in “Prodigies” (Feb. 10), an Apple TV romantic comedy about two former wunderkinds, played by Will Sharpe and Ayo Edebiri, reëvaluating the relationship that they’ve been in since they were nine. Beneath all the precocity might be a more consoling idea: that falling short is its own kind of charm.—Inkoo Kang

paragraphs.text: Dolly’s Musical, a Rocking Galileo
sentences: Dolly’s Musical, a Rocking Galileo

paragraphs.text: As fall whirls into winter, bracing depictions of people accused of horrific crimes hit Broadway. Bruce Norris’s “Downstate” portrays convicted sex offenders (Booth; in previews); Tectonic Theatre Project’s documentary play “Here There Are Blueberries” examines Nazi life at Auschwitz during the Second World War (Barrymore; previews begin Nov. 2); and Suzie Miller’s “Inter Alia” examines the fallout of a rape accusation against a teen-ager whose mother is a criminal-court judge (Music Box; Nov. 10). In this dark wake come frothier crowd-pleasers, including the magic show “Now You See Me Live” (Hirschfeld; Nov. 11), inspired by the eponymous film franchise, and “Galileo” (Shubert; Nov. 10), a rock musical starring Raúl Esparza as everyone’s favorite anti-authority scientist. The latter is followed by two other bio-musicals: “Dolly,” for which Parton wrote new songs to accompany her standards (St. James; Dec. 7), and the West End transfer of Jamie Lloyd’s stripped-down “Evita” (Winter Garden; Feb. 27), the 1978 Andrew Lloyd Webber–Tim Rice megahit, with Rachel Zegler as Argentina’s galvanizing former First Lady.

paragraphs.text: In the New Year, two star-powered solo shows spotlight moments from the past: in Jessica Dickey’s “The Amish Project,” Jonathan Groff plays several members of a rural Pennsylvania community coping with a 2006 school shooting (Broadhurst; Feb. 10), and Manfred Karge’s “Man to Man” sees Tilda Swinton reprise a role she originated in English, in 1987—a widow who begins passing as her dead husband in nineteen-thirties Germany (Lucille Lortel; Feb. 21). Clifford Odets’s 1935 “Awake and Sing!” (Friedman; Dec. 15) dramatizes the same period in New York, via a family of Jewish immigrants; this revival’s powerhouse cast includes Danny Burstein, Jessica Hecht, and Jeremy Shamos. The complexities of family life in early-twentieth-century N.Y.C. also shape “Imitation of Life” (the Shed; Nov. 21), a musical adaptation, by John Legend and Lynn Nottage, of the eponymous Fannie Hurst novel and Douglas Sirk film. It juxtaposes two single mothers, one Black and one white (Adrienne Warren and Jessica Vosk), each raising a daughter.

paragraphs.text: Winding the clock back further is a remounting of “Spring Awakening” (Studio Seaview; Nov. 27), about frisky teens bucking authority in an eighteen-nineties German town, with music by the late Duncan Sheik. Youthful passions also flummox the elders in “Dirty Dancing” (Horne; Feb. 12), a musicalization of the iconic eighties film. The script flips in Sarah Ruhl’s “Faydra” (New York City Center Stage 1; Feb. 2), a reimagining of the mythical princess (played by Julianne Moore) stricken with lust for her stepson-to-be. If only she could decompress at the silent meditation retreat in Bess Wohl’s “Small Mouth Sounds” (Barrymore; Feb. 18), getting a starry revival with Julia Roberts, Paul Rudd, Sarah Paulson, and Greta Lee.

paragraphs.text: Dominique Morisseau’s “Mix and Master” (Haimes; Jan. 5) has the all-too-rare distinction of being a new play on Broadway. It concerns a d.j. desperate to keep the Bronx’s last record store in business, and stars Kara Young and Ruben Santiago-Hudson. Cutting-edge works fill the Under the Radar festival (Jan. 6-24), including “Yoroboshi” (Japan Society; Jan. 14-16), a Japanese folktale retold through disturbing Barbie cosplay. The festival also hosts a second run of this fall’s “America, Who Hurt You?” (Public; Jan. 6), in which the Tony-winning Sarah Jones embodies nineteen characters to critique our “low-key mid-apocalyptic moment.”—Dan Stahl

paragraphs.text: Youth will be served in the season’s movies, as in “Club Kid” (opening Nov. 6), a comedy directed by and starring Jordan Firstman, in which a gay New York party promoter discovers that he fathered a son a decade ago and is given custody of the boy (played by Reggie Absolom). A teeming cast energizes Marine Atlan’s “La Gradiva” (Dec. 18), about a group of French high-school students on a field trip to Naples that exacerbates conflicts and identity crises. Yet old age, too, is a major subject of new releases, as in the octogenarian Mike Leigh’s “Tender Loving Care” (Dec. 4), which he says will be his last film, about a social worker who brings a colleague along on a visit to her elderly parents and finds them in physical decline. Ryûsuke Hamaguchi’s “All of a Sudden” (Nov. 25) stars Virginie Efira as a manager of a French elder-care facility, whose new friendship with a visiting Japanese theatre director (Tao Okamoto) proves both personally and professionally rewarding.

paragraphs.text: Movies about movies are perennial enticements to filmmakers, as in “I Play Rocky” (Nov. 6), about the young Sylvester Stallone (Anthony Ippolito), a little-known actor whose signature screenplay nearly went unproduced because of his insistence on starring in the film. Quentin Tarantino wrote the script for “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” (Nov. 25), a sequel to his 2019 film “Once Upon a Time . . . in Hollywood,” but he didn’t direct the new installment; David Fincher did, and Brad Pitt returns as the titular stuntman, now working behind the scenes. Pedro Almodóvar’s “Bitter Christmas” (Nov. 13) is an intricate and passionate double melodrama, in which a 2004 tale of a filmmaker (Bárbara Lennie)—who’s written a script based on a friend’s life—is actually a movie by a current-day director (Leonardo Sbaraglia) who’s done the same thing.

paragraphs.text: Other forms of the art life figure prominently, as in “Everybody Digs Bill Evans” (Dec. 4), Grant Gee’s tightly targeted bio-pic of the jazz pianist (Anders Danielsen Lie), who, in 1961, paused his career after the sudden death of his trio’s bassist. Another bio-pic, “Elsinore” (Nov. 20), depicts the actor Ian Charleson (Andrew Scott) as he struggled to perform in a production of “Hamlet,” in 1989, while weakened by AIDS. Jesse Eisenberg wrote and directed “The Debut” (Dec. 11), in which Julianne Moore plays a community-theatre actress who approaches a bit part surprisingly earnestly. “Behemoth!” (Dec. 4), written and directed by Tony Gilroy, stars Pedro Pascal as a cellist returning to Los Angeles to care for his ailing mother (JoBeth Williams) and forced to confront his past. In Judd Apatow’s comedy “The Comeback King” (Feb. 5), Glen Powell plays a former country-music star who attempts to rebuild his life by pursuing a college degree.

paragraphs.text: Ancient Greece, Two Triennials
sentences: Ancient Greece, Two Triennials

paragraphs.text: This winter in New York’s art world is, more than usual, a season of extremes: you can see works that are incredibly old and others that are brand new—and, of course, much in between. One end of the spectrum is represented by the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s “Across Wine-Dark Seas: Art and Identity Beyond Ancient Greece” (opening Dec. 20). The exhibition aims to reconsider ancient Greek art by asking: Who were the Greeks interacting with as they sailed throughout the Mediterranean? How did they view those people, and how did those cultures influence them? If recent “Odyssey” mania was a bellwether, then this show of roughly a hundred and eighty objects, with sources including some twenty-nine international lenders, should be a hit.

paragraphs.text: Not as old but still classic is the Neue Galerie’s collection of twentieth-century Austrian and German art. The museum was closed all summer for renovation, and “25th Anniversary Exhibition: Masterworks from the Neue Galerie” (Nov. 12) marks its full reopening. A trip to the Neue is an experience of exquisite comfort: you can feast your eyes on works such as Gustav Klimt’s glittering “Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer I” (1907) and then treat yourself to a delicious tart at the museum’s Viennese-style café.

paragraphs.text: If novelty is more your thing, contemporary art is also on the menu. The Museum of the City of New York puts on “The Photography Triennial: After Dark” (Nov. 20). Last time, the focus was turned inward toward the home; this time, thirty-three artists train their lenses on New York City’s night life. A few months later, the New Museum opens “The Outside Expands” (Feb. 4), the sixth edition of its triennial, which spotlights early-career international artists. The show’s themes, listed in the press release, are impenetrably vague, but it should be eye-opening to see work by thirty-six up-and-coming artists, most of whom are exhibiting in a U.S. museum for the first time.

paragraphs.text: Two of the season’s most enticing exhibitions offer micro-histories of specific categories of art. MOMA PS1’s “Hard Art” (Nov. 5) traces Black abstract painting from 1969 to the present—a subject ripe for critical inquiry. It features still underappreciated artists from a pioneering generation alongside more contemporary practitioners, taking an expanded view of painting in the process. Meanwhile, the Whitney Museum is devoting an entire floor to digital art—a feat not often attempted at brick-and-mortar institutions. “Artport: A History of Internet Art” (Nov. 21) is a retrospective of the Whitney’s online gallery of the same name, which has featured more than a hundred commissions in the past twenty-five years. This exhibition includes multiple cohorts of practitioners who have navigated a field that remains marginalized by the mainstream art world.

MOMA PS1’s “Hard Art”
(Nov. 5) traces Black abstract painting from 1969 to the present—a subject ripe for critical inquiry.
It features still underappreciated artists from a pioneering generation alongside more contemporary practitioners, taking an expanded view of painting in the process.
Meanwhile, the Whitney Museum is devoting an entire floor to digital art—a feat not often attempted at brick-and-mortar institutions.
“Artport: A History of Internet Art”
(Nov. 21) is a retrospective of the Whitney’s online gallery of the same name, which has featured more than a hundred commissions in the past twenty-five years.

paragraphs.text: Of course, no art season is complete without solo shows. The most substantial of these is “Jess: A Dialogue of Presences” (Feb. 19), a survey, at the Drawing Center, of the hermetic artist Jess Collins, who went only by his first name. The exhibition concentrates on his dizzyingly complex collages—which he called “paste-ups”—along with the community that he and his partner, the poet Robert Duncan, formed around their home, in San Francisco. Meanwhile, several museums are homing in on niche aspects of canonical artists’ careers. The Cooper-Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum offers “Frederic Church in Jamaica” (Oct. 30), showcasing the artist’s rarely seen sketches from an 1865 trip to the Caribbean country; the Noguchi Museum’s “No Ordinary Light: Akari at 75” (Nov. 4) looks at the history of Isamu Noguchi’s once controversial, now beloved paper lamps; and the Morgan Library’s “William Blake: Paradise Lost” (Feb. 26) examines the influence that the poet John Milton had on the visionary artist.—Jillian Steinhauer

(He danced for years for the choreographer Ohad Naharin, whose technique seems to turn his dances inside out.) A recent work, “Touch of RED,” locked two men in a battle that suggested violence, love, and the ecstatic release of club dancing. Pitts has described it as “primitive, wonderful, groovy, wild,” which also describes his over-all vibe.

paragraphs.text: There is an infinite appetite for balletic versions of “Romeo and Juliet,” driven by the headlong rush of its love story and the cinematic sweep of Sergei Prokofiev’s score. New York City Ballet, at the start of its winter season (David H. Koch Theatre; Jan. 19-Feb. 28), replaces its current, rather soulless production, by Peter Martins, with a poetic one by Alexei Ratmansky, in which the characters explode with life, and the streets of Verona erupt in kaleidoscopic formations. At the end of the season, Taylor Stanley, a dancer whose fluidity and delicacy have always set him apart, will give his farewell performance, which includes Jerome Robbins’s otherworldly “Opus 19/The Dreamer” and a new solo by Kyle Abraham.—Marina Harss

paragraphs.text: The composer Annea Lockwood is only a bit younger than “Density 21.5”—the defining modernist flute miniature written by Edgard Varèse, in 1936. That piece marks the origin—and, in its centennial, the destination—of the flutist Claire Chase’s twenty-four-year-long commissioning program, Density 2036. Varèse’s piece is named for the density of platinum (in approximate grams per cubic centimetre). Lockwood, in contrast, has spent her life making music from more transient properties: the sounds of vibrating glass, of desiccating trees, of a burning piano. “Elwha!,” her contribution to Chase’s project, premières at the Kitchen (Dec. 11-12), with Chase playing flutes of seven kinds in concert with field recordings of Washington State’s Elwha River. Lockwood’s “Sound Map of the Columbia River,” created with the trumpeter Nate Wooley, will have its first performance two months later, at Roulette (Feb. 5).

paragraphs.text: Sarah Chamberlain, the president and C.E.O. of the Republican Main Street Partnership, was observing a focus group of MAGA voters in Colorado in late August when she first started to hear a surge of complaints about government corruption. Chamberlain’s organization is dedicated to electing House Republicans—it began with a moderate orientation but has been adjusting to the new world of Trump voters—and she was in the state to help insure that the MAGA faithful would turn out in close races. At that meeting of voters and at subsequent ones, Chamberlain recalled, “we didn’t prompt them. It just came up.” She added, “They are tired of watching their members of Congress get wealthy, and they’re struggling to fill their gas tanks.”

paragraphs.text: Corruption is always a tempting message for the party out of power. Donald Trump used that playbook in 2016, vowing to drain the Washington swamp. Bemoaning corruption is risk-free: no voters are in favor of it, even if they have differing interpretations of what the term entails. In the meantime, hitting corruption lets the opposition party duck the harder tasks of producing a detailed legislative agenda. But, in this cycle, what could catapult the issue from a topic of chronic bellyaching to an actual mechanism for changing votes is the gloomy economic climate. Voters who are feeling flush may be willing to tolerate a degree of self-dealing from politicians that becomes insupportable when grocery bills are high. Corruption “is always a useful word, but it’s more effective at some times than others,” Robert Boatright, a political-science professor at Clark University and the co-author of the 2025 book “American Corruption Talk,” noted. “It’s a way to put your finger on people’s general dissatisfaction with our politicians, with our economy, with the state of the world.”

paragraphs.text: Then, there is the matter of President Trump. Chamberlain said that Trump did not come up in her focus groups, though participants did cite Donald, Jr.,’s oligarch-financed post-wedding festivities, along with stock trading by the husband of the former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi—this was a maga crowd, after all. But it doesn’t take much to imagine that the swirl of self-dealing around Trump—the Qatari jet gifted for the President’s use; the millions paid to Melania Trump’s production company for her documentary; a billion-plus in crypto profits that flowed into the family coffers—contributed to the fury. Indeed, in a Washington Post/ABC News/Ipsos poll released on October 18th, sixty-six per cent of voters said that they believed Trump was using the Presidency for personal gain, up from fifty-six per cent a year earlier. Ominously for Republicans, the shift came largely from G.O.P. voters and Republican-leaning independents.

paragraphs.text: Even with an already cynical electorate, the toll is measurable. In September, Gallup found that Americans’ perception of corruption in government was at its highest level in two decades of polling; eighty-nine per cent said that it is widespread, up ten percentage points from a year earlier. And the blame is not spread evenly. In an A.P.-NORC poll from September, forty-nine per cent of respondents said that the word “corrupt” describes Republicans extremely or very well; just thirty-seven per cent took that view of Democrats.

paragraphs.text: Little wonder, then, that Democrats have jumped on the issue. According to the tracking firm AdImpact, Democrats have spent a hundred and eighty-two million dollars this year on corruption-focussed advertising in House and Senate races—far more than Republicans have and more than Democrats did during the previous four elections combined. Their strategy is not simply to highlight corruption but to link it to economic consequences. As a September memo from the Senate Majority PAC, the main super PAC backing Senate Democrats, advised, “The strongest reason to vote against a Republican continues to be that they have raised our costs; do not sacrifice the cost piece in favor of communicating about corruption alone, as corruption charges that are not anchored to costs do not clear the bar.” Hence an ad run against Michael Whatley, the G.O.P. candidate for an open Senate seat in North Carolina: “He got rich lobbying for Big Oil, while they jacked up prices on you.”

(Collins has denied any wrongdoing.) “Maybe there’s a reason Susan Collins does anything Donald Trump wants her to,” a woman who looks like she’s straight out of an L. L. Bean catalogue says to the camera. chapters.title: The Party Girls at the Heart of “Club Kid”
chapters.section: The Talk of the Town · The Pictures
chapters.subtitle: Jordan Firstman’s directorial début tells the story of a gay promoter who finds out he’s a father. On a groggy Lower East Side morning, the three actors who play his night-life posse compare notes on queer family planning.

paragraphs.text: Early on a recent Thursday, three of the stars of Jordan Firstman’s directorial début, “Club Kid,” were recovering from weeks of celebratory partying with caffeinated beverages in Seward Park, on the Lower East Side, near where much of the film takes place. A few older Chinese women were doing Tai Chi as a man in protective earmuffs and a neon vest blasted a leaf blower. The actors—Alaska Riley, Benny Jean Pierce, and Saturn Risin9—decided to take a stroll. Riley, sipping a chai, had been up for an hour; Pierce, latte in hand, had awoken at six to exercise; Saturn, holding a matcha, was unslept, having flown in from Los Angeles the night before and gone straight to the Swan Room for oysters and caviar fries. Firstman had cast all three for their real-life involvement in New York’s night-life scene.

chapters.title: Reliving the Bronx’s Biggest Battle
chapters.section: The Talk of the Town · Time Travel Dept.
chapters.subtitle: In 1776, Continental Army soldiers defended what is now Glover’s Rock from the British. The other day, reënactors did it all again at Orchard Beach.

paragraphs.text: You’re reading The Talk of the Town: fun, fizzy dispatches from the city and beyond.
sentences: You’re reading The Talk of the Town: fun, fizzy dispatches from the city and beyond.

paragraphs.text: Glover’s Rock, a glacial erratic boulder in Pelham Bay Park, in the Bronx, pushes through the tree branches around it like the prow of a beached ship. The Parks Department has put up an identifying marker next to a pullout on the road leading past the rock to Orchard Beach or to City Island. Two hundred and fifty years ago, the biggest battle ever fought in the Bronx began here. At dawn on October 18, 1776, four thousand British and Hessian soldiers marched along the narrow country road that followed the high ground the rock sits on. They had come ashore nearby and were trying to encircle Washington’s army from the east as he attempted to get out of a dangerous position on Manhattan and escape across the Hudson River to New Jersey.

paragraphs.text: A plaque on the rock says it was named for Colonel John Glover. He commanded four regiments, a total of eight hundred men, which occupied defensive positions along the road. The odds in this fight were five to one, at best. Glover came from Boston, and his New England troops not only fought as infantry but also provided Washington with whaleboats and oarsmen when he needed them. The boat in which he is standing in the painting “Washington Crossing the Delaware” was theirs.

Improvising, he ordered three of his regiments to hide behind stone walls that lined the road. An advance guard stood in formation near the rock, ready to meet the British. The fourth regiment he put farther back along the road, in reserve.

paragraphs.text: Sunrise, according to contemporary sources, was at 6:32 A.M. Two hundred and fifty years later, on Sunday, October 18, 2026, first light came at about 6:30. At that hour, Glover’s Rock is a lonely sentinel. A street light shaped like a “Y” casts bluish light over the boulder and an adjacent patch of lawn. Cars go by only occasionally. On the morning of the anniversary, four deer emerged from a reed thicket next to the lawn, and two Canada geese flew by. At 7:11, the sun came up blazingly over Long Island Sound, breaking through places in the previously all-dark tree line.

paragraphs.text: By ten o’clock, about a thousand people had shown up to watch a reënactment of the battle, sponsored by local historical societies, civic groups, and schools. For logistical reasons, it had to be held in Orchard Beach Park. Spectators crowded the beach’s promenade. A somewhat tall ship—a two-masted schooner called the Lynx—sailed in on the morning’s mild breeze and anchored offshore. Reënactors dressed as British soldiers got in a dory and rowed from the schooner to the beach’s edge. Then they rowed back and forth for a while. A member of the U.S. Coast Guard, who had been standing on the beach in a life vest to help them disembark, walked back to a tent on the promenade. “They don’t want to get wet,” he said. The dory rowed back to the Lynx.

Opposing them were Continental reënactors led by Sean Grady, of Westchester, who impersonated Colonel Glover impeccably, down to the Boston accent. “We cannot expect any rein-fahce-ments!” he said.

Glover and his men held them up long enough for the whole army to get away.

chapters.title: Dante de Blasio Is Off Vocal Rest
chapters.section: The Talk of the Town · Dumb Luck Dept.
chapters.subtitle: As a newborn, the son of the former mayor won free music lessons for life at the Brooklyn Conservatory of Music—and then he quit. Now he’s finding his way back to the notes.

paragraphs.text: You’re reading The Talk of the Town: fun, fizzy dispatches from the city and beyond.

paragraphs.text: Maternity wards are inherently stressful places. But on the night of September 3, 1997, the stakes were especially high for expectant parents. A few weeks earlier, the Brooklyn Conservatory of Music had decided that the first local baby born on the school’s hundredth birthday would receive a lifetime of free music lessons. The anniversary date was September 4th. About ninety babies are born in Brooklyn every day. To locate the winner, B.K.C.M. employees called hospitals around the borough until they found their lucky newborn, at Brooklyn Methodist: a little boy by the name of Dante de Blasio—yes, relation.

It had come about largely out of guilt. “I started taking lessons around age eight, I think—I’ll have to ask my dad,” he said. “I just remember the rage. I was very stubborn and had no musical talent.” (His father, the former New York City mayor Bill de Blasio, clarified: “He was positively sour.”) Among piano, guitar, and singing, piano was the worst. “It was the social element,” Dante said. “I did not like being told what to do.” He quit after less than a year.

chapters.title: New Jersey, the Diesel State
chapters.section: The Talk of the Town · Dept. of Contamination
chapters.subtitle: A data center in the Meadowlands recently leaked five thousand gallons of fuel into a nearby creek. The Riverkeeper of the Hackensack gives a tour.

paragraphs.text: You’re reading The Talk of the Town: fun, fizzy dispatches from the city and beyond.
sentences: You’re reading The Talk of the Town: fun, fizzy dispatches from the city and beyond.

paragraphs.text: For people who worry about the health of the New Jersey Meadowlands, the giant tidal estuary that is the brackish heart of the Hudson-Raritan watershed, it was a complicated summer. During the FIFA World Cup, MetLife Stadium, built on what was once essentially an island in the middle of marshes, was described by organizers as being in a mythical-sounding land called “New York New Jersey.” Then, last month, five thousand gallons of diesel leaked from a Secaucus data center that nobody really knew was there into a creek just off the Hackensack River, and suddenly, as guys in hazmat suits swarmed the noxious water, it was back to seeing the Meadowlands as both properly in New Jersey and a dumping ground.

paragraphs.text: Even New Jersey’s environmental officials downplayed the spill’s impact. But not Bill Sheehan, the Hackensack Riverkeeper. “The people talking for the people who spilled the diesel are saying that none of it got out here in the river,” Sheehan said the other day, as he floated up the Hackensack on a thirty-foot pontoon boat. He was nearing some orange booms that blocked the entrance to Anderson Creek Marsh, at the mouth of the contaminated waterway. “I don’t know how that’s possible, since it took them something like fourteen hours to get these booms set up.”

paragraphs.text: It was nearly high tide, and Sheehan was taking two scientists out to perform water-quality readings. Born and raised in Secaucus, Sheehan, who is seventy-seven and founded the Hackensack Riverkeeper advocacy organization in 1997, was wearing a hoodie and aviators; his white hair and horseshoe mustache made his silver hoop earring read “pirate.” As the scientists readied their monitoring devices, Sheehan steered, cranking classic rock on the boat’s radio. The floating booms, to starboard, looked like flimsy protection against the spill. “I know data centers are suddenly the cause célèbre, or whatever,” he said. “But the damn thing was over there for twenty-five years and nobody cared, and nobody told me about the danger. I thought Data was a character on ‘Star Trek’!”

The scientists ducked as the boat floated beneath a rusty drawbridge, completed in 1911 and designed by Joseph Strauss, the Golden Gate Bridge’s chief engineer. Picking up speed, Sheehan noted a fourteen-story hotel—windows all broken, rooms gutted. “It used to be the Crowne Plaza,” he said. “I busted them because I found out they were dumping raw sewage in the river three times a week. They pled guilty, and took the Crowne Plaza name off it.” Lately, he’s been hearing that it will be “a Class A hotel.” “We’ll see,” he said.

paragraphs.text: The radio played Zeppelin, Petty, and Bruce as the scientists took readings under a Route 46 bridge. The temperature and the dissolved-oxygen levels weren’t great, but they weren’t terrible; back at their labs, the scientists would test for nutrients and fecal bacteria. (The lower Hackensack is an E.P.A. Superfund site.) They tested under the Turnpike, near a Bergen County sewage-treatment plant, and then in Kingsland Marsh, a wide tidal wetland filled with delicate spartina grass, which marks good food and habitat for aquatic life of even the most microscopic kind. The marsh had the day’s best readings; being there felt like being on Cape Cod.

He was frustrated with the newfound outrage over data centers, which he reckoned had more to do with utility bills than with larger water-quality concerns. He planned to urge the state to file a Natural Resource Damage claim, as it had in 1994, after a barge carrying more than three hundred thousand gallons of caustic-soda solution overturned. “That’s the active ingredient in Drano,” he said. Settlements for that spill—combined with settlements for groundwater chromium contamination and for an Exxon oil spill in the Arthur Kill—restored wetlands in Jersey City. A former dump got rehabilitated. “We also got a nine-hole public golf course, for people that want to shoot white balls around for no good reason, at the princely sum of about thirty dollars a round,” Sheehan said. “On the Hudson River side, they’ve got to pay half a million dollars to join those clubs. I call this one the People’s Golf Course.”

chapters.title: An Exiled Filmmaker’s Unsparing View of Contemporary Russia
chapters.subtitle: Andrey Zvyagintsev’s “Minotaur” is the first independent feature to portray Russian life during the war with Ukraine.

paragraphs.text: Gleb is a successful businessman, a Russian muzhik made good—wealthy, sturdy, practical—who owns a logistics company in a midsize, provincial city. His employees respect his competence and his no-nonsense direction; in turn, he looks after them, a stern but caring paternal figure. At home, things are different. His wife, Galina, a noble beauty, excels at the role of the plumed bird in a cage and yet suffers for it, fumbling around awkwardly for an escape. They are emotionally estranged but inexorably codependent, circling and watching each other in their tasteful lakefront home.

paragraphs.text: Two dilemmas that threaten to upend Gleb’s life emerge early in “Minotaur,” the new film by Andrey Zvyagintsev, the most celebrated Russian director of his generation, whose previous two movies were nominated for Best Foreign Language Film at the Academy Awards. “Minotaur” is set in the fictional city of Krasnoborsk in the fall of 2022, half a year into Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, when Vladimir Putin announced a so-called partial mobilization, or military draft. At the headquarters of Gleb’s company, workers huddle around a phone, watching a chaotic scene at the Russia-Georgia border. Thousands of Russian men fleeing the country to avoid being called up to fight are trying to cross, causing an enormous traffic jam. “Holy fuck,” one of Gleb’s employees says. Seven of them have already left; others are planning to.

paragraphs.text: This is one of the few glimpses that the film offers of the Special Military Operation, as Russia’s war in Ukraine is known in official parlance. The others are subtle, likely to be missed by an untrained eye: a parked car has a “Z” decal—an early symbol of the invasion adopted as a show of support—on its rear window; at a crosswalk, the camera lingers on a woman pushing a wounded veteran in a wheelchair. “The war unfolds on the periphery,” Zvyagintsev told me recently. “That was exactly the state of mind, the atmosphere, that defined the start of the conflict. Everything was hushed up—everything was taboo.”

The couple gets into bed with an icy distance between them. A boozy dinner out with friends turns awkward and then, back home, ugly. “I’m tired of being your shadow,” Galina says. The plotline is borrowed from “La Femme Infidèle” (“The Unfaithful Wife”), a 1969 French psychological thriller, directed by Claude Chabrol. Like the husband in that film, Gleb sets out to uncover what he already knows.

paragraphs.text: The war in Ukraine, meanwhile, is closing in on him, too. The mayor of Krasnoborsk is demanding that Gleb and a handful of other local business leaders draw upon their employees to provide a quota of men for the invasion. The higher-ups in Moscow have made their needs clear, and the mayor dutifully transmits them. “We aren’t here to bargain,” he says. It’s impossible to know what Gleb thinks about the war. What matters is the narrow personal implications. “Can’t they achieve this without us?” he asks the mayor. They can’t—draft lists must be submitted by next Thursday or the state will start sweeping up men on its own. “He stays silent,” Zvyagintsev said, of Gleb. “Just sitting there with a total poker face.”

paragraphs.text: Zvyagintsev is not an overtly political filmmaker, but his movies are unsparing in their portrayal of life in contemporary Russia. “He’s a meticulous director, for whom mise en scène is absolutely central,” Joël Chapron, a French film historian who first met Zvyagintsev in the early two-thousands, told me. Varvara Shmykova, an actress who has had supporting roles in two of Zvyagintsev’s films, including “Minotaur,” said that Zvyagintsev doesn’t believe in the “magic of cinema,” in which miracles happen spontaneously during filming. Rather, she said, he “composes and shoots each frame with textbook precision.” The paradox, Shmykova continued, is that all this control produces something that feels uncannily genuine: “He manages to transfer the feeling of life itself onto the screen.”

paragraphs.text: Iris Lebedeva, who plays Galina, called Zvyagintsev’s process an “enormous puzzle, a moving mosaic.” She told me about shooting an early scene in which Gleb drives her character to a café. He suspects that her plan to get a coffee before a haircut is cover for a rendezvous with a lover. Zvyagintsev had “imagined how it all should be beforehand,” Lebedeva said. “That this tree has to stand here and be exactly this tall, with its leaves moving in just this way. That far off in one corner, behind a window, people should sit drinking coffee from exactly this kind of cup. That a couple with a little dog should walk past, at precisely this rhythm.” As the scene unfolded, she went on, “I realized that, even though I was playing the lead, I was no more important in the frame than that tree, or these passersby, or that particular building. All of it exists in order to create a larger whole.”

Reality is painful for him, but he’s not afraid of it.”

paragraphs.text: Ultimately, Gleb is forced to make an offering to the state: fourteen draftees for the war. The number is a gesture at the movie’s titular allusion. According to Greek mythology, every nine years Athens had to send fourteen young people to the Minotaur’s labyrinth, in Crete, where they were devoured as sacrificial victims. The implication is that power preserves itself at the expense of its subjects. Zvyagintsev paraphrased Gleb’s reaction to being drawn into Russia’s war effort: “Damn, why do I have to deal with this?” Gleb, he went on, “wants to stay on neutral ground, to not get involved, to keep from getting sucked into this nightmare.”

paragraphs.text: Zvyagintsev and I met this summer in Jurmala, a charming Latvian resort town on the Baltic Sea. He had filmed “Minotaur” in Riga, Latvia’s capital, a thirty-minute drive away, and was now spending a month at a rented house on a quiet lane, with a footpath leading through a patch of pine trees to the shore. “Minotaur” would have its theatrical release in the fall—November 20th in the United States—and Zvyagintsev was at work on a book about his directorial career. He treated my visits as a welcome distraction, and we spent the better part of several afternoons sitting in wooden deck chairs, nursing a pot of tea, and munching on local strawberries.

paragraphs.text: Zvyagintsev is sixty-two years old, with a shadow of a silver beard and chunky black eyeglasses. His gaze is intense yet fundamentally kind—he would regularly check to see if I was cold, hungry, or in need of a ride. He is intimidatingly well read, in the way of the Russian intelligentsia—one evening, at a garden party, I spotted him reading a translation of the Aeschylus play “The Persians”—but without coming across as haughty or pretentious. Zvyagintsev, unlike many prominent Russian filmmakers, was not born into the country’s cultural élite: he grew up in Novosibirsk, in Siberia, and was brought up by a single mother who taught Russian language and literature at a local school. Zvyagintsev “comes from below,” and is interested in the world of ordinary people, Dolin told me. “In the lives of mechanics and plumbers, he sees something mythological.”

I arrived early, and, as I waited, he sent me a text message about where we should sit: “Ask whether the table in the corner is free—not the one diagonally across, all the way in the back, but just opposite the entrance. That spot is nice: it’s by the window, you get the sunset, and there’s more air than in the middle of the room.”

paragraphs.text: Over dinner, I asked him about his childhood in Novosibirsk. Zvyagintsev’s father abandoned the family when Zvyagintsev was five years old. “A man of no fixed occupation,” Zvyagintsev said. He was a sculptor, a high-school gym teacher, a police officer. Then, one day, he was gone. Still, Zvyagintsev recalled an otherwise happy childhood in the Soviet Union of the nineteen-sixties and seventies: hanging out in the courtyard of his apartment block, playing soccer with friends, performing at a local youth theatre. When he was eighteen, his father made an unannounced visit to the apartment where Zvyagintsev lived with his mother. They exchanged an awkward hug but barely spoke. Zvyagintsev later learned that his parents had argued that day. His father asked his mother what Zvyagintsev was up to. She said that he was studying acting, at a drama academy in Novosibirsk. His father erupted. “What kind of nonsense is that?” he said, slamming his fist on the kitchen table.

She said that he was studying acting, at a drama academy in Novosibirsk.
His father erupted.

Antonioni’s great innovation was that the story line fades away, along with conventional expectations about action, time, and dramatic resolution. Psychological tension and narrative development come not from plot but from silence, duration, landscape, and movement. “My mind was blown,” Zvyagintsev said. “I understood then that a film can be incredibly rich and meaningful even when hardly any action happens.”

paragraphs.text: After graduation, Zvyagintsev found a job as a dvornik, a street cleaner. “You’d get up early in the morning, sweep up some cigarette butts, and the rest of the day belonged to you,” he said. He spent most afternoons at the newly opened Museum of Cinema, which hosted retrospectives on German Expressionists and the French New Wave, and regularly showed the works of modern auteurs, from Fassbinder to Kurosawa. The idea of making films of his own still seemed far-fetched—that was for people with the right diplomas and connections. But then, when Zvyagintsev was twenty-seven, the Soviet Union collapsed, taking with it a rigid system of top-down management and state-directed job assignments. “It was a tremendous time,” he said. “Everyone was free to do as they pleased, try out what they liked.”

paragraphs.text: Eventually, he began to direct commercials—for a shoe store, a granite workshop, the soccer club Spartak. Through a campaign for REN TV, an independent television network launched in the mid-nineties, he met Dmitry Lesnevsky, who ran the channel with his mother. At the time, Lesnevsky was looking for directors to work on “The Black Room,” a psychological drama series, with each episode unfolding in a confined, claustrophobic space. The minimalist format was a necessity, Lesnevsky told me, because “we didn’t have the money to make real films.” He gave Zvyagintsev a handful of scripts, and Zvyagintsev picked one about a wealthy banker and his bodyguard. He filmed it quickly, on a budget of a couple of thousand dollars. “To my amazement, from this rather absurd and ridiculous premise appeared something with style, air, atmosphere—everything we would see later in Andrey’s films,” Lesnevsky said. Zvyagintsev remembers Lesnevsky telling him, “Good job, you turned shit into candy.”

paragraphs.text: “Lamentation Over the Dead Christ,” an Italian Renaissance masterwork by Andrea Mantegna which shows Christ lying on a marble funeral slab, is known for its extreme foreshortening. Christ’s feet are closest to the viewer, and his head and torso are enlarged beyond normal proportions. The effect is highly corporeal, a naturalistic confrontation with the immediacy of death. Zvyagintsev first saw the painting in an art-history class at the drama academy in Novosibirsk. It inspired a framing shot that comes nine minutes into “The Return,” Zvyagintsev’s first full-length feature: two brothers tiptoe into a hallway, having learned that their father, who has been missing for twelve years, has come home.

paragraphs.text: “The Return,” based on another script procured by Lesnevsky, was filmed near Lake Ladoga, north of St. Petersburg. The landscape is dotted with abandoned structures, decaying artifacts of a vanished civilization: a diving platform looming over a glassy lake, a rickety wooden observation tower. The father takes his two sons—Ivan and Andrey—on a camping trip that becomes something of a Biblical quest, a test of will and belief. The action, like God’s creation of the world, takes place over seven days. Ivan, the younger son, is doubtful and skeptical of his father, whereas Andrey, the elder, is faithful and trusting—the twin archetypes of man’s relation to the divine. “Two neophytes going through an initiation rite,” Zvyagintsev said. The film ends in tragedy: a death that is both sacrifice and atonement. We never learn the father’s name.

paragraphs.text: In September, 2003, “The Return” was shown at the Venice Film Festival, where it won not only an award for best début but also the Golden Lion, the festival’s top prize. Two months later, Zvyagintsev got a call from the Kremlin, inviting him to meet with Putin, who was then in his first term as President. “There will be tea, something to eat—you’ll sit down and have a chat,” Zvyagintsev said, recalling the summons. In a reception room at Putin’s residence, facing a suite of television cameras, the two had a scripted conversation that lasted barely a few minutes. “He said, ‘Congratulations,’ and that was it,” Zvyagintsev said. “The camera crews left.”

paragraphs.text: Zvyagintsev’s indifference to official power made him unusual for a Russian artist, especially in the age of Putin. Filmmaking is expensive, and for many people in the industry the Russian government is both a source of funding and a powerful facilitator. “Plenty of other directors would have pissed themselves with happiness,” Lesnevsky said. “But for Andrey it was awkward, as if one imperious nod from the tsar in his direction risked casting a shadow on the purity of his artistic expression.”

paragraphs.text: On June 4, 2004, Marvin Heemeyer drove what the media later dubbed the “Killdozer” on a two-hour rampage through the streets of Granby, Colorado. Heemeyer owned a muffler shop in the town and had been engaged in a long-running series of property and zoning disputes with local authorities. He eventually lost, and then spent several months converting a bulldozer into an improvised armored vehicle, adding steel plates and gun ports. His spree ended when the Killdozer got stuck in the wreckage of a collapsed building; as police approached, Heemeyer shot himself. Zvyagintsev heard about the story during a trip to New York. “This initial impulse, the basic conflict, made quite an impression,” he told me. “The desire for revenge, a thirst for retribution, for justice.”

paragraphs.text: Back in Moscow, he and Oleg Negin, a frequent collaborator, began drafting the screenplay for what would become his fourth feature, “Leviathan,” a story of a man’s confrontation with an indomitable system, framed around his battle to save his home from demolition at the hands of corrupt local bureaucrats. In an early version, Zvyagintsev imagined a final scene in which Nikolay, the Russian Heemeyer, bursts out of his garage riding a bulldozer and uses it to topple an excavator. But that felt both too technically complex—“Who was going to give us an excavator to destroy?” Zvyagintsev said—and tonally wrong. His world view is harsher. “In Andrey’s films, God is silent and never intervenes,” Alexander Rodnyansky, Zvyagintsev’s longtime producing partner, said. “No one is granted miracles or hears a voice from Heaven, and no one is saved.”

paragraphs.text: For the location of “Leviathan,” Zvyagintsev considered several towns outside Moscow, and some as far away as Belarus. Nothing felt quite right, though, until Andrey Ponkratov, Zvyagintsev’s longtime production designer, discovered Teriberka, a remote Arctic fishing settlement on the northern coast of Russia’s Kola Peninsula, which Zvyagintsev called an “outpost of archaic reality.” The coastline is severe, with boulder-strewn beaches and granite cliffs stabbing into icy waters. Away from the shore, the tundra is barren, a broad expanse of moss, lichen, and exposed rock. When Zvyagintsev first visited Teriberka, in 2012, a local driver told him about humpback whales that, in early summer, are visible from shore. Zvyagintsev thought it was a sign: “We came with a film called ‘Leviathan,’ and it turns out this place has actual whales.”

paragraphs.text: The film’s central motif came from the Book of Job, the story of an upright, God-fearing man who faces tragedy and suffering seemingly without reason. The Biblical story speaks elliptically of a Leviathan, a giant sea creature beyond human control: “Upon earth there is not his like, who is made without fear.” To Zvyagintsev, modern Russia looked like the embodiment of yet another “Leviathan”—that of Thomas Hobbes, who imagined the sovereign state as an immense power entrusted by its subjects to protect them from disorder and violence. In Zvyagintsev’s film, the state machine, rather than protect the individual, crushes him. That’s a universal dynamic, Zvyagintsev insisted, “only in Russia it’s more blatant, visible right on the surface.”

paragraphs.text: Before “Leviathan” premièred, at the Cannes Film Festival, in 2014, Zvyagintsev and Rodnyansky hosted a private screening at the Russian Ministry of Culture, which had provided more than a million dollars of the film’s budget. The funding was less a financial necessity than a political wager. “It seemed to me that simply having the words ‘Made with the support of the Ministry of Culture of the Russian Federation’ in the opening credits would protect us and provide a certain degree of cover,” Rodnyansky said. The Minister of Culture at the time, Vladimir Medinsky, was a conservative ideologue. After watching the film, he called Zvyagintsev into his office. “Why do you insist on painting Russia with a black brush?” he asked. “Why not use brighter colors?” Zvyagintsev replied that an artist merely represents the reality around him. “We’re not in charge—you are,” he said. “When life gets better, when things in the country change, then there will be a brighter side, and I’ll reflect that, too.”

paragraphs.text: On the morning of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, in February, 2022, Zvyagintsev was in a hospital room in Germany. The previous June, during a COVID wave in Moscow, his wife, Anna Matveeva, a photographer and a film editor, had caught the virus, and Zvyagintsev, who had a long-standing lung condition and was fearful of falling ill, went to stay in his office. After a week, he decided to get a shot of Sputnik V, Russia’s COVID vaccine. Within days, his temperature had spiked and he was racked with body aches and exhaustion. His doctor sent some blood samples for analysis. “Every single measure was wildly abnormal,” Matveeva told me. paragraphs.text: For Zvyagintsev, making a movie in Europe meant relearning much of his usual process. In Russia, Rodnyansky, his producer, had protected him from the fraught and unseemly aspects of securing financing. “He spoiled me,” Zvyagintsev said. “If he said yes, then that was enough.” But, in Europe, art-house dramas of the type Zvyagintsev makes are financed piecemeal, through an arrangement of co-producers, public subsidies, broadcasters, and private investors. “How much do things cost, how to find the money to pay for them, how to find outside investors and present your ideas to them—none of that existed for him back in Russia,” Karmitz said. “Andrey had to learn an entirely new system.”

chapters.title: Why Immigration Agents Don’t Quit in Protest

paragraphs.text: In the winter of 2018, Joshua Childress was sent to the Yuma Regional Medical Center, in southwest Arizona, to guard a man who’d fallen from a thirty-foot-high border wall. Childress was in his seventh year in the United States Border Patrol and had grown accustomed to doing hospital watch, in which agents monitor recently apprehended migrants to insure that they don’t escape while receiving care. To Childress’s surprise, the injured man spoke fluent English. Childress asked why he had come to the U.S. “Because this is my home,” the man replied.

Childress was in his seventh year in the United States Border Patrol and had grown accustomed to doing hospital watch, in which agents monitor recently apprehended migrants to insure that they don’t escape while receiving care.
To Childress’s surprise, the injured man spoke fluent English.
Childress asked why he had come to the U.S. “Because this is my home,” the man replied.

paragraphs.text: The man, who appeared to be in his early twenties, had lived in Arizona since he was eight years old—longer than Childress had been in the state himself. A few months earlier, the man had hosted a barbecue at his house, and neighbors had called in a noise complaint. The police came, asked for the man’s I.D., and reported him to immigration authorities, who deported him to Mexico. Childress asked why the man hadn’t sought Dreamer status under the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program, which provides protection from deportation for certain undocumented immigrants brought to the U.S. as children. The man explained that he had wanted to, but his father had been afraid that the paperwork was a trick meant to entrap them.

I’ve been down there wandering around for three months, trying to figure out what to do, and I decided, You know what? I’ll take my chances and come back here. And then I fell from the fence and broke my leg.”

paragraphs.text: Like all agents, Childress had come face to face with countless migrants; he was familiar with their struggles. But he was adept at pushing aside stories of misfortune to focus instead on the border crossers who had serious criminal histories—the arrests he felt good about. Increasingly, however, Childress had begun to question whether the vast majority of the migrants he encountered, most of whom had come to the country to change tires or pick lettuce or work in construction, really posed a threat. Once, a man at the Yuma processing center had removed his shirt to show Childress marks on his back, where he had been whipped by smugglers after he refused to carry a bundle of drugs across the border. The lashes, it occurred to Childress later, were “Christlike.”

This, after all, was the job.

paragraphs.text: I first heard of Childress in the fall of 2018, when reading an article that he wrote for the Daily Beast titled “Why I Quit the Border Patrol.” “I ultimately realized that I was putting people in cages for non-violent offenses, something I opposed in every other area of the law,” he wrote. “I was impeding the movement of people when I wanted to be able to move freely around the world. I was enforcing the rules of a game I had won simply by being born on the right side of a line.”

paragraphs.text: Reading Childress’s account was like looking in a rearview mirror. I had quit the Border Patrol for similar reasons in 2012, after nearly four years as an agent, and had spent the next phase of my life trying to make sense of my participation in the militarized violence of immigration enforcement, working as a barista and a bartender while attending school to become a writer and a teacher. Childress’s departure from the Border Patrol came shortly after the implementation of Donald Trump’s “zero-tolerance policy,” under which parents were separated from their children at the border, sparking a national uproar. At the time, it was possible to believe that agents’ understanding of their work might be changing.

paragraphs.text: That summer, more than a dozen Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents signed a letter to the Secretary of Homeland Security, Kirstjen Nielsen, calling for the agency to be disbanded. In July of 2019, Jenn Budd, who had resigned from the Border Patrol nearly two decades earlier, wrote an “Open Letter from an Ex-Border Patrol Agent,” calling on current agents to demand change or quit in protest of the immoral orders that they were being asked to carry out. The following year, Wesley Farris, a high-ranking member of the Border Patrol’s notoriously hard-line union, spoke out against the zero-tolerance policy, telling PBS’s “Frontline” that separating children from their parents “was the most horrible thing I’ve ever done.” But remarkably few agents followed in Childress’s footsteps; Farris, for example, refused to participate in separations but did not quit, asking his supervisor to assign him elsewhere instead.

paragraphs.text: Much of the outcry stirred by the harsh policies of the first Trump Administration was quelled by Joe Biden’s promise of a more measured approach. His Presidency saw a record increase in migrant encounters at the border, a fact that is often attributed to lax enforcement. In fact, the Biden Administration left several of Trump’s restrictionist policies in place, and detentions at the border increased twelvefold while total removals tripled. Still, there was a feeling among immigration agents that they were being shackled by the new Administration. By 2024, the Border Patrol had lost a quarter of its workforce, with many longtime agents opting for early retirement. They often blamed the President. “Under Biden, things are the worst they have ever been by far,” one agent told the Washington Examiner, adding, “Agents are afraid of ending up on the news for doing their job or getting in trouble for doing their job. There is no morale.”

paragraphs.text: With Trump back in the White House, many agents now regard the Administration as once again on their side. But the demands of meeting its overarching goal—deporting a million people a year, per Trump’s top domestic-policy adviser, Stephen Miller—have led to a new form of strain. In 2025, The Atlantic reported that ICE’s workforce “has never been so miserable.” Employees have become burned out and morally conflicted as their focus has shifted from pursuing drug smugglers and human traffickers to apprehending asylum seekers in courthouses and arresting day laborers at their worksites. Another agent said that he was contemplating quitting rather than continuing to spend his days “arresting gardeners.”

paragraphs.text: In early 2026, after the murders of Renee Good and Alex Pretti during Operation Metro Surge, in Minneapolis, the journalist Ken Klippenstein reported that many immigration agents were “getting seriously paranoid” about the public backlash to the shootings. The operation was so unpopular with the rank and file that Border Patrol and ICE struggled to find personnel for the deployment. By July, morale among immigration officers had dipped below its nadir during the Biden Administration, with agents now complaining of being overextended, inundated with novice recruits, and undermined by inflammatory rhetoric from on high. Agents said that they had previously found motivation in their jobs by “being able to stop bad people and narcotics from coming in,” and expressed frustration that the Administration’s political posturing was distracting from their duty to “protect the public” and to focus on “the very worst of the worst.”

paragraphs.text: The sociologist Irene Vega, in her 2025 book “Bordering on Indifference,” draws on a series of interviews with Border Patrol and ICE agents to analyze the “moral economy” of the immigration-enforcement workforce. From the moment agents arrive at the federal law-enforcement academy, she writes, they “are trained and socialized as police officers, and taught that their raison d’être is to protect America by preventing the entrance and executing the removal of noncitizens deemed unwanted by the state.” The inherently bureaucratic nature of enforcing immigration law has always been at odds with the paramilitary image that is sold to most recruits. Agents prepare for violent criminal encounters and cultivate a “warrior mentality” despite the fact that they are most often, as Vega writes, “at war with an enemy that does not fight back.”

paragraphs.text: Many agents who have quit for moral reasons cite this tension. In a 2019 article for The American Scholar, Brendan Lenihan, a former Border Patrol agent, wrote, “The federal government taught me how to shoot an assault rifle from a moving vehicle and how to fast-rope from a hovering helicopter, but never did anyone explain how to go home at the end of a shift and forget about the migrants I’d apprehended and their stories.” As with Childress, the accumulation of nonthreatening encounters eventually made his job untenable. “I left the Border Patrol because I was exhausted by the tragic stories,” he wrote, “and because the more I saw, the less affected I was by events that had once seemed shocking.”

paragraphs.text: How is it, then, that so few agents seem to arrive at this moral breaking point? Nearly two-thirds of Americans disapprove of the Trump Administration’s immigration crackdown. It has become customary for agents to mask their faces from public view—D.H.S. maintains that this is to prevent doxing, but it is also emblematic of a growing perception of this work as shameful. In off-duty social situations, agents often obscure what they do to avoid awkwardness and scorn, even hiding the nature of their employment on dating apps. “We can’t always support what happens just because it’s one of us,” a Border Patrol agent had told a private group chat in the wake of Pretti’s killing. And yet, even as their work has grown increasingly cruel, there has been no exodus of agents who reject it.

paragraphs.text: Last spring, I began reaching out to my former co-workers to hear about their recent experiences in the job. The first who agreed to speak with me, an agent who now works for ICE, suggested that we meet at a diner in Arizona. It had been years since we’d seen each other; in greeting, we clasped hands and embraced. Over coffee, we talked about our families, and he asked about my life as a university professor. Gradually, our conversation turned to our old colleagues. He caught me up on who was still in the Border Patrol, who had transferred to the Canadian border, and who, like him, had gone to work for ICE. Many of my former co-workers, I learned, had become fathers; others had succumbed to alcoholism. A few, he told me, had died by suicide.

As he saw it, morale was good, far better than under Biden—his office had more resources and had expanded with new hires, many of whom had backgrounds in law enforcement and were hard workers. There were caveats, of course. He did not like being sent to arrest people at courthouses during immigration and asylum hearings, which felt like a trick. He thought that it had been a bad idea to send border agents to Minneapolis, since they were accustomed to patrolling barren deserts, “where everybody is an illegal,” and not trained to police the population of an inner city. One, a fellow-Latino whom I’d always known to be sensitive in his treatment of migrants, told me that he “agreed with the mission but not the tactics.” An agent who was still working at the southern border said that, in recent years, ICE agents have become increasingly hostile toward the people they are arresting. “The growth in abuse of rank and authority has become so distorted that due process no longer exists,” he told me, adding that standards of agent accountability had reached new lows.

paragraphs.text: Despite their qualms, none of the agents I spoke to—many of whom were nearly eligible for retirement—disagreed with current policies strongly enough to leave. But one of them mentioned Aaron Veckey, a former agent who, in 2024, gave a series of interviews to the right-wing media personality James O’Keefe. While in the patrol, Veckey had raised concerns about detention conditions with his superiors, who repeatedly dismissed the issue. He filed a whistle-blower complaint with the U.S. Office of Special Counsel and soon received a cease-and-desist order for “reporting sensitive information outside of Border Patrol,” a charge he was cleared of after an internal investigation. With O’Keefe, he spoke of the “dogma of apathy” that prevailed among agents and compared the treatment of migrants at his station to the torture at Abu Ghraib.

paragraphs.text: As far as I know, Veckey, who was then less than a year from retirement, is the only non-anonymous active-duty agent to publicly blow the whistle on the agency’s inhumane treatment of migrants. Over the phone, he described images from the peak of asylum-seeker arrivals, in 2023 and 2024, that continued to haunt him. As many as six hundred migrants were detained outdoors without shade in his station’s parking lot and sally port, where temperatures reached a hundred and fifteen degrees in the summer and dipped below freezing in winter. He recalled a night when he found sixty migrants piled on top of one another for warmth. Another agent had shown him a photo of a half-dozen migrants jammed in a porta-potty to share body heat. Despite the freezing temperatures, agents confiscated the migrants’ coats and refused to give them blankets. Veckey remembered being ordered to remove jackets from breast-feeding mothers.

In Chicago, hundreds of migrants were held for three or more days in facilities not meant for overnight detention; at the Mesa airport, in Arizona, more than seven hundred people were crowded into a deportation staging facility with a maximum capacity of two hundred and three. In downtown Manhattan, as many as eighty-six people were crammed for three or more days at a time into a temporary holding room on the tenth floor of 26 Federal Plaza. It was one of four immigration-detention spaces at the courthouse, which are designed to hold no more than twenty-two people combined. The Washington Post called the room “a closet of humanity that smelled of sweat, urine and feces.”

paragraphs.text: The brutality of American immigration enforcement is nothing new. The U.S. Border Patrol was created with the passage of the Immigration Act of 1924, a piece of legislation championed by nativist politicians and self-professed eugenicists. The act, which imposed strict quotas on legal migration from Europe and banned migration from Asia altogether, exempted Mexico to appease U.S. agricultural interests and created the Border Patrol to police crossings and to insure that workers left the U.S. after the harvests. Early agents were often former enforcers of the Chinese Exclusion Act—“Chinese Inspectors” and “Mounted Guards”—and ex-Texas Rangers, who’d become notorious during the previous decade for terrorizing borderland Mexicans in a lynching campaign known as La Matanza. Many, too, were active members of the Ku Klux Klan.

Their clothes and other belongings were fumigated with Zyklon B, a cyanide-based pesticide later used in Nazi gas chambers.

paragraphs.text: In the 1983 book “The Tarnished Door,” the investigative reporter John Crewdson detailed a litany of abusive tactics employed by the Immigration and Naturalization Service, the predecessor of ICE and C.B.P., including handcuffing migrants to moving cars, stealing their valuables, extorting them for sex and money, and pushing them off cliffs and then disguising their deaths as accidents. Crewdson described the agency as “shot through with nepotism, incompetence, corruption, and brutality” and recounted incidents of “men with drawn guns knocking on bedroom windows, shining flashlights on couples in bed, climbing in windows and barging through doors without permission, and taking occupants (usually aliens, sometimes citizens) away in various stages of undress.’’ Establishing total control of the border and immigration, he concluded, could never be achieved “short of the establishment of a police state.”

paragraphs.text: After 9/11, the war on terror wedded immigration enforcement to national security. The I.N.S. was dissolved, and its workforce was split across three agencies under the newly formed Department of Homeland Security: ICE, the Border Patrol, and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. Along with the bureaucratic reshuffling came a surge in funding and recruitment. Veterans of the conflicts in Afghanistan and Iraq, in particular, found post-deployment work in the new enforcement apparatus. In many cases, they were using the same military equipment and technology that they’d used in the fight against Al Qaeda and the Taliban.

paragraphs.text: Joshua Childress and I met on a bright spring morning in a Phoenix café not far from his home. The café was owned by Greek immigrants, he told me, and he’d heard about it at the Eastern Orthodox church where he worshipped and worked as a handyman. We ordered freddo espressos and soon began sharing stories of the low-level abuse and malfeasance we had witnessed in the patrol. Childress recalled how senior agents insinuated that trainees could mount searches and make arrests based on little more than a gut feeling, how a perceived aggression could be used to justify almost any use of force, and how the word of agents was almost always trusted over the testimony of the people they apprehended. “I knew things were messed up as I was doing them, as I was learning them,” Childress told me. “But I was justifying it. You learn during training how to word things so it doesn’t sound like you’re doing what you’re actually doing.”

paragraphs.text: The Border Patrol began implementing Trump’s zero-tolerance policy in May of 2018. “I kind of wish I had planted my flag at that point and said, ‘No, no more,’ ” Childress told me. But his wife had recently lost her job, and the couple had twin boys starting at a new school. They decided to delay his resignation, and he stayed on for several more months. Driving in and out of the parking lot each day, he noticed that many of his colleagues’ vehicles had Don’t tread on me bumper stickers. Childress recalled thinking, They don’t realize they’re the boot. In the end, he said, “it wasn’t so much that I changed my mind as I started to be honest with myself.”

paragraphs.text: When I asked Childress why he thought more agents didn’t quit, he quoted Upton Sinclair: “It is difficult to get a man to understand something when his salary depends on his not understanding it.” Indeed, in many ways, there has never been a more lucrative time to be an immigration agent or a more costly time to quit. As part of Trump’s hiring push, new recruits enjoy up to fifty thousand dollars in signing bonuses on top of starting pay that ranges from sixty to ninety thousand dollars. Agents who stay on earn tens of thousands in retention bonuses, and those who rejoin after retirement can receive pension pay along with their salary. Most ICE and Border Patrol agents can expect to make about a hundred thousand dollars after just three years in the job, with many earning nearly two hundred thousand a year by the time they retire.

paragraphs.text: In 2021, I attended an online panel co-hosted by the group Veterans for Peace. The event commemorated the fiftieth anniversary of the Winter Soldier Investigation, organized by Vietnam Veterans Against the War, in which more than a hundred veterans spoke publicly about war crimes they had witnessed or participated in. paragraphs.text: Brittany DeBarros is the organizing director of About Face: Veterans Against the War, which she describes as a support network for post-9/11 veterans who were “disturbed by the gap between what they’d witnessed and what the American people were being told.” About Face offers veterans a way to navigate shame, guilt, and rage by “standing in the truth of the harm you’ve done,” something that DeBarros, a veteran herself, found liberating. The existence of such groups creates what political scientists call a permission structure: a framework that offers people an opening to change their mind or their behavior and to embrace new, or deeply buried, ideals. In About Face, veterans find community in the shared experience and morals that caused them to reject the systems in which they once perpetuated suffering.

chapters.title: The Year Math Changed Forever

paragraphs.text: A mathematician is a machine for turning coffee into theorems. This was a line often invoked by the Hungarian mathematician Paul Erdős, who was fuelled by coffee and amphetamines, slept little, travelled near-constantly, never married or had children, and published almost fifteen hundred papers in his lifetime, in collaboration with hundreds of other mathematicians. But Erdős was, in most ways, not machinelike. He called lecturing in mathematics “preaching,” woke friends at odd hours by asking, “Is your brain open?,” wore only silk underclothing on account of his sensitive skin, and claimed not to have learned how to butter toast until he was twenty-one. He gave away most of his earnings to charitable causes and to young mathematicians in need of funds for their education, and he offered bounties (sometimes ten dollars, sometimes a thousand) for solutions to mathematical problems he’d proposed. Mathematics was his life. Mathematicians were his family. It has been said that, even above his remarkable contributions to the mathematical literature, he helped the discipline most profoundly by turning people who might otherwise have become hedge-fund managers or F.B.I. agents or lost souls into mathematicians. When he died, in 1996, at the age of eighty-three, he left behind about a thousand problems. Solving an Erdős problem is a great honor, as is having a low “Erdős number,” a term that describes how many degrees of separation one is from having published work with him.

paragraphs.text: Terence Tao was ten years old when Erdős visited his home town of Adelaide, Australia, in 1985. Erdős loved children and called them epsilons. Tao, a mathematics prodigy, had started taking college-level courses at age nine. Erdős posed a problem for him and Tao to work on together. A photograph of their meeting, taken by Tao’s mother (who had been a math teacher before having kids), shows the young mathematician and the old one deep in thought, hands at chins, looking at the notepad before them. “I wish I remembered more about the encounter,” Tao recently said. Erdős later sent the Tao family a note, handwritten on Bell Labs stationery, that, after brief wishes of a good New Year, reiterated the problem they had discussed: “Let 1 ≤ a1 < a2 < . . . atn ≤ n be a sequence of integers . . .”

paragraphs.text: In May of 2023, the mathematician Thomas Bloom began gathering the known remaining unsolved Erdős problems on a website, erdosproblems.com. Their depth and difficulty vary, deliberately. Erdős described some of them as “marshmallows” and others as “acorns.” In a talk in February of this year, titled “Machine Assistance and the Future of Research Mathematics,” Tao quoted Erdős’s characterization of a marshmallow as “a tasty tidbit supplying a few moments of fleeting enjoyment,” and of an acorn as “requiring deep and subtle new insights from which a mighty oak can develop.”

paragraphs.text: The role that artificial intelligence will play in research mathematics has been talked about a fair amount in the past five years, and a fearsome, unbounded amount in the past five months. Tao—a professor of mathematics at the University of California, Los Angeles, and a founder, in 2025, of the Foundation for Science and AI Research—has been one of the most prominent voices in this discussion. This is in part because he is a venerated mathematician who won a Fields Medal, the highest honor in the discipline, at age thirty-one; in part because, like Erdős, he is especially collaborative and community-oriented; and in part because he was already thinking seriously and publicly about A.I. when many of his peers still thought, as Tao put it, “Oh, it’s a toy, it makes so many mistakes, it’s never going to be useful.” A.I. labs such as Google DeepMind, OpenAI, and Anthropic were trying to demonstrate otherwise. From their perspective, math problems are practical benchmarks to measure the capabilities of their products. Mathematical proofs can be digitized and objectively verified, and the field of mathematics is highly respected. Early on, A.I. tools were conspicuously bad at basic math. When OpenAI’s GPT-4 Turbo was asked to count the number of “L”s in “lollapalooza,” it answered “Five.” The tools have since improved dramatically, but even now L.L.M.s find difficult some tasks that we find easy, and vice versa. “The means by which an A.I. solves a problem is just so orthogonal to the way a human solves a problem,” Tao said, in a recent lecture. A.I. proofs often devote pages to what would be obvious to an undergraduate, then offer only a few lines on what to a human mathematician is a large, cloudy move.
