paragraphs.text: In 2024, A.I. tools began performing well at the International Mathematical Olympiad, scoring at the silver-medal level and, in 2025, at the gold level. Only top high-school students and a handful of prodigies participate in the I.M.O. (Tao won a bronze at age ten, a silver at age eleven, and a gold the next year. His longtime friend and mathematical collaborator Allen Knutson recalled how an ex-girlfriend who had been on Mexico’s I.M.O. team told him about an annoying little kid with a stuffed animal who would come out of the exams saying, “Too easy”—it was Tao.) Then, in early 2026, mathematicians and math hobbyists using A.I. tools started solving some of the more marshmallowy Erdős problems. In January, GPT-5.2 Pro appeared to have solved Erdős Problem #728 largely on its own; Tao and others took on the necessary task of verifying the proof. Then more Erdős problems began to fall. Tao explained that some of these problems had remained unsolved on account of “an attention bottleneck,” meaning that no one had given much thought to them; others were problems that had already been solved, but the solutions were not widely known, and the A.I. had effectively retrieved them. But, on May 20th, OpenAI published a proof of Erdős Problem #90, the unit-distance problem, a combinatorics problem that involves arranging points on a plane so that as many pairs as possible are spaced an equal distance apart. This was not a marshmallow. Top-level mathematicians had spent time on it, nudging it forward.

paragraphs.text: Then, there was the Navier-Stokes existence-and-smoothness problem. The problem has to do with how a set of equations that model the movement of fluids seems to imply solutions with infinite speed, which should be impossible. In 2000, the Clay Mathematics Institute, in Cambridge, Massachusetts, had announced seven Millennium Prize Problems, chosen and formulated by the institute’s Scientific Advisory Board, each with a million-dollar award for solving it. The Millennium Prize Problems are acorn problems, and Navier-Stokes was one of them. On September 8th, OpenAI announced that it had solved it. Much of the mathematical community, which was already distressed, tipped over into existential crisis.

paragraphs.text: “I have had the strangest week ever in my life,” Tao declared at the start of a talk he gave three days later, at Caltech. Usually, when lecturing, he appears in a collared shirt, tucked in. At this talk, he wore jeans and a black T-shirt. The shirt featured the Edo-era woodblock print “Under the Wave Off Kanagawa,” a famed art work noted for its fractal-like patterning—the wave comprises smaller, similarly shaped waves, which themselves comprise yet smaller ones. “Ordinarily, I would use A.I. and create some fancy version of this,” Tao said, gesturing at the bare-bones graphic on the screen behind him. “I used PowerPoint,” he admitted, to laughter. He then described the current state of the field. Solutions were being published, often with little explanation or detail, relying on the good will and free labor of mathematicians to verify and illuminate them. A.I.-generated submissions were overwhelming mathematics journals and databases, and the field’s genteel ecosystem of people volunteering their time to referee submissions was collapsing under the weight of slop. Sometimes even the person submitting the paper did not understand it. Answers were being found, but, in math, answers are often not very important; the insights and inventions that arise while working toward an answer matter much more. “We have to slow down,” Tao said. “It’s insane, the pace.” During the Q. & A. portion of the talk, an audience member observed that A.I. has thus far been solving problems that already exist. Where did Tao think new problems would come from? New problems, Tao said, emerge from “the slow, deliberative process” of working toward a solution, “and this is what’s being destroyed.”

paragraphs.text: In another era of mathematics, which is to say, in April, I visited Tao at his office in the Mathematical Sciences Building at U.C.L.A. The building was connected through a mazelike series of corridors and stairs to Boelter Hall, where, in 1969, the first message was sent on ARPANET, the precursor to the internet. One of the hallways had a telephone booth. Tao’s office was spacious and mostly unadorned, with beige carpeting and a beige sofa, six blackboards mounted onto two long walls, and stacks and shelves with hundreds of books bearing titles such as “Advances in Analysis: The Legacy of Elias M. Stein,” “Number Theory Volume I: Tools and Diophantine Equations,” and “The Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves.” Near the light switch, there was a drawing of a toothy monster in a black suit and tie, next to a message in code (“LWKIRLCS,” part of it read) written on a sheet of paper. His oldest child had made it for him years ago. “I don’t think I remember how to decode it,” Tao said. None of his many prizes and honors were on display, but there was a wall hanging—made by the Mathematics Genealogy Project, of North Dakota State University—recording generations upon generations of who had studied under whom.

The building was connected through a mazelike series of corridors and stairs to Boelter Hall, where, in 1969, the first message was sent on ARPANET, the precursor to the internet.
One of the hallways had a telephone booth.

Tao’s office was spacious and mostly unadorned, with beige carpeting and a beige sofa, six blackboards mounted onto two long walls, and stacks and shelves with hundreds of books bearing titles such as “Advances in Analysis: The Legacy of Elias M. Stein,”
“Number Theory Volume I: Tools and Diophantine Equations,” and “The Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves.”
Near the light switch, there was a drawing of a toothy monster in a black suit and tie, next to a message in code (“LWKIRLCS,” part of it read) written on a sheet of paper.
His oldest child had made it for him years ago.
“I don’t think I remember how to decode it,”
Tao said.

None of his many prizes and honors were on display, but there was a wall hanging—made by the Mathematics Genealogy Project, of North Dakota State University—recording generations upon generations of who had studied under whom.

paragraphs.text: Tao is slim, wears his dark hair boyishly grown out, and has a gentle and calm demeanor. He is fifty-one but looks a decade younger. He rides a bike to work, and he has several tennis racquets in the corner of his office, though he said that he hasn’t really had time to play tennis in years, owing to his proliferating duties. “If you want to profile a mathematician, I’m maybe not a good example,” he told me. “I get to do math on Tuesdays and Thursdays. And sometimes on airplanes.” He lives with his wife, Laura, their two children, four cats, a dog, and three rabbits. The family had intended to give the oldest rabbit, Spumpkin, away to a friend, because Spumpkin was “traumatized by the traffic” outside their house, Tao said. But that didn’t work out, so Spumpkin is still with them, which is O.K.; Spumpkin and the oldest cat are close friends.

paragraphs.text: Many mathematical geniuses have been as celebrated for their eccentricity as for their work. Erdős is only one of many examples. The eighteenth-century Italian mathematician Maria Agnesi, who wrote an early textbook on calculus, gave away most of her money and abandoned mathematics to devote herself fully to theology. The logician Kurt Gödel, whose incompleteness theorems revealed that no mathematical system could express every mathematical truth, came to believe that doctors had a secret book in which they wrote honestly about medications, that the I.R.S. was after him, and that his friend who had died decades before was still alive in the Soviet Union. John Nash (famous for contributions to game theory), Grigori Perelman (famous for solving the Poincaré conjecture), and Alexander Grothendieck (famous for developing a new foundation for algebraic geometry) all dramatically withdrew from their social spheres. Tao does not fit this tradition. He is very much of the world, which is somewhat surprising, considering that, when he was two years old, he was reportedly found typing out a favorite children’s story on his dad’s typewriter.

paragraphs.text: As a kid, Tao imagined that what professional mathematicians did was solve problems assigned to them, sort of like homework. By age seventeen, he was a graduate student in the mathematics department at Princeton University, and still somewhat in the dark about what he was meant to do with his mathematical imagination. He played a lot of video games, easily completed his coursework, and almost failed the qualifying exam for his doctorate. Not all child prodigies go on to brilliant careers. Tao, however, went on to become one of the most revered mathematicians alive today, praised for his profound contributions to an astonishing range of subjects, from the study of numbers to the analysis of waves—a polymath of math.

paragraphs.text: The election of Donald Trump for a second term, in 2024, made Tao even busier. Federal funding for U.C.L.A.’s Institute for Pure and Applied Mathematics (IPAM), where he serves as the director of special projects, was frozen, as were National Science Foundation grants that supported his department’s research, including his own. And, as the Trump Administration unrolled various anti-immigration orders, students and postdocs had visa troubles. Tao spent many months fund-raising among private donors to support the stipends and T.A. positions relied upon by his graduate students. Some of these donors were hedge funds and banks that had in the past offered him large sums to work for them. He had always declined, “but those connections were useful in that moment,” he said.

paragraphs.text: One of the companies that offered funding to IPAM was OpenAI. Earlier this year, Tao was interviewed alongside an OpenAI executive, Mark Chen, in what the company called a fireside chat. In the interview, Tao expressed both hopes and concerns about A.I. in mathematics; OpenAI later used some of his bullish bits in a promotional video, which featured Tao saying that A.I. is “ready for prime time,” and that it will reduce cognitive friction “down to zero.” Tao has collaborated with researchers at Google DeepMind, and one of his projects was sponsored by the A.I. startup Math, Inc. For these reasons, among others, he was for a time portrayed as almost uncritically enthusiastic about the role of A.I. in math; in a June article in Quanta Magazine, he was described as an “evangelist.”

paragraphs.text: It is true that, for a few years now, Tao has suggested that the chalkboard-dominated field of mathematics might be overdue for change. He has expressed hope that A.I. could help make a “living spreadsheet” of mathematics, which could self-update as new mathematical discoveries are made; he has worked to develop open-source A.I. tools, in addition to helping organize events to encourage a collaborative approach to A.I. In 2024, he started the Equational Theories Project, which involved dozens of professional and amateur mathematicians who, with the assistance of A.I., tried to determine the truth or falsity of about twenty-two million mathematical implications of some forty-five hundred invented mathematical laws. He has spoken about how A.I. could enable even more large-scale collaborations. He would like mathematics to be able to ask questions more in the tradition of biologists’ population studies (“What makes lemur populations rise and fall?”) rather than case studies (“What can we say about this particular lemur and from there gain some insight into lemurs in general?”).

paragraphs.text: Recently, though, Tao’s muted optimism has given way to alarm. He has begun to speak in praise of cognitive friction, and has described A.I. companies as having “managed to optimize by removing all the humanity out of the process.” In his office, he told me, “We have to actively experiment and figure out what works for us. Because otherwise what’s going to happen is that the tech companies will release these products—you know, ‘Here’s my artificial scientist’—and there’ll be no competing products.” He doesn’t advocate that mathematicians avoid using A.I. But, at his lecture at Caltech, he pointed out that the effect of A.I. on math followed what he called nonlinear dynamics. He went on, “Any kind of monotone, one-dimensional thinking—Oh, a little bit of this is good, therefore a lot of it is going to be a lot better—one of the lessons of math is that most systems don’t work like that.” Human understanding needed to remain central. For example, with a proof written by a human, he noted, “you can talk to that person and say, ‘What was your experience? What was your inspiration?’ You have some insight into the process. They can give talks. And, years later, they’ll still be in the community, and they can pass on their expertise to their students. They contribute to the whole ecosystem of mathematics.”

paragraphs.text: In his office, Tao had compared the crisis that the mathematical community was facing to the transition that cities underwent when the horse and buggy was replaced with the car. “You need parts of the city that are still for pedestrians and parts that make sense for travelling by car. But you can’t have the whole city designed to be optimal for cars,” he said. “Because no one wants to live in that city.” This was an analogy he used often in talks and interviews. In a more recent talk, he recalled his reliance on the analogy with a slide demarcating lanes for pedestrians and ones for automobiles. “This is where we want to go,” he said. “But, unfortunately, this is sort of where we are now—” He advanced to a slide that depicted people running away in terror from what appeared to be autonomous machines.

paragraphs.text: Much of the math we learn as kids is mechanical, which may be why mathematics is sometimes misperceived as an unimaginative field. A more accurate understanding might come from recalling that Charles Dodgson, better known as Lewis Carroll, was a professional mathematician. In some ways, the writing of “Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland” resembles mathematical research. Mechanical calculation, in this analogy, is the basics of composition: spelling, subject-verb agreement. But, in order to explore logic and whimsy and wonder and paradox, Carroll invented characters like the White Rabbit, the Cheshire Cat, and the Queen of Hearts, and situations like the Mad Tea Party and the Caucus Race. These characters and scenes are akin to the objects and techniques mathematicians invent as they explore mathematical ideas. When Andrew Wiles proved Fermat’s Last Theorem, more than three hundred and fifty years after its initial postulation, mathematicians were thrilled, but not because of the answer, which wasn’t surprising. (No, there are no positive whole numbers such that an + bn = cn if n > 2.) What was wonderful about Wiles’s proof was the mathematical techniques he’d developed along the way. That was what advanced mathematics.

paragraphs.text: But coming up with characters and story lines is challenging—which is probably why it’s satisfying. I sat in on a meeting Tao had with his postdoctoral mentee, Iqra Altaf, who was working on a problem in geometric-measure theory. “Mathematically, the news is not good,” Altaf said. She went to the chalkboard and began writing out a counterexample to a conjecture she had thought would prove true. “Math is like a video game, or like ‘Groundhog Day,’ ” Tao said. “Every time you die, you come back.” En route to failure, you learn something that aids you in the next go-around. He quoted the Russian mathematician Vladimir Arnold, who once said, “Mathematics is the part of physics where experiments are cheap.” In another conversation, Tao compared learning mathematics to watching “Emily in Paris,” a show that he and his wife enjoyed. “It’s completely ridiculous fluff, but it’s also fun. You learn the tropes, and you can kind of see how it’s going to go,” he said. “But if you’re just given a synopsis of the plot, like, ‘Here’s the premise, and this is what happens’—that’s not the point.” And, if you want to learn how to write your own show, “then it’s not helpful at all.” Seeing scenes done poorly and done well, watching how plots are resolved even in formulaic shows—that’s how you learn to direct your own series. Among the crises that the arrival of A.I. has brought to mathematics, “the most urgent one is, How are we going to train our graduate students?” Tao said. It is a question that he has been asking for several years. The modest-sized problems that graduate students would once have spent months on—learning to think mathematically in the process—can now sometimes be solved by A.I. tools in hours.

paragraphs.text: On October 9th, Tao gave a talk (another!) hosted by the American Institute of Mathematics. Three days earlier, OpenAI had released three hundred and seventy-two additional results contributing to or solving open problems in mathematics. (OpenAI’s statement announcing the results briefly mentioned that four thousand problems had been tried, but that detail didn’t get much notice.) Tao started out by explaining that, when he had been invited to give the talk, a year earlier, the title of it had been “Machine Assisted Proof”—that was, in fact, the title on the posters advertising the event—but that “by this point the idea that machines could assist proof was maybe not quite as novel.” So he changed the title to “Math 2.0.”

paragraphs.text: Math 1.0—“math up to 2025,” Tao said—operated under the basic assumption of “proof scarcity.” Proofs were a sort of currency, central to publishing papers, winning prizes, and getting jobs. The landscape had now changed to one of proof abundance, which Tao compared to food abundance, when “you become a bit pickier about what food gets crammed into your mouth.” We would soon be living in a vast sea of low-quality A.I. proofs, with mathematicians left to fish out what was worthwhile. Math 2.0 would follow from figuring out “how to actually integrate A.I. and humans” to “find a new frontier of tasks,” only some of which would be problems.

paragraphs.text: The mathematician Geordie Williamson, of the University of Sydney, in Australia, described one A.I.-assisted solution to me as “like this beautiful thing for the whole math community” and another as “like the weed killer Roundup being sprayed on a garden.” Both results were published by Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic. The beautiful thing concerned an eighty-seven-year-old problem, the Jacobian conjecture. We can think of the problem as having to do with the possibility of a one-to-one mapping from one shape to another. On July 19th, the day of the Spain-Argentina soccer game, Alpöge posted on X, “hello there the jacobian conjecture is false thanx to my close friend akhil”—a human—“for asking about it and my other close friend fable”—an A.I. model—“for working during the world cup final.” Claude Fable 5 had produced a counterexample to the conjecture, much like how an ostrich is a counterexample to the conjecture that all birds can fly. Williamson said, “Within thirty-six hours, mathematicians had kind of understood where the counterexample comes from and why it’s natural.” A handful of mathematicians, including Tao, explored the proof, came to understand it—a process that I kept hearing mathematicians refer to as proof digestion—and reconstructed the algebraic geometry that underlay it. On July 21st, Tao posted the work on his blog, including the transcript of a conversation he’d had with ChatGPT as he looked into the details. By July 22nd, Semon Rezchikov, of Barnard College, had created a visualization of the counterexample using only high-school-level mathematics. The proof had opened up thinking, not decapitated it.

paragraphs.text: But then there was Williamson’s Roundup story: On August 12th, Alpöge posted again, though it was not immediately clear what the new disclosure was about. “It was this crazy tweet, just a whole sequence of pluses and minuses. It looked like a secret code,” Williamson told me. He soon recognized that it was the next in a series of what are called Hadamard matrices. The first few Hadamard matrices had been described in 1867, and the matrices have fascinated mathematicians ever since, with breakthroughs and new insights turning up every couple of decades or so, the most recent in 2004. At a talk not long before, Williamson had been encouraging mathematicians to find the next one. Then there it was, on X. “At first, I was, like, Awesome,” Williamson told me. But then he saw that Alpöge had posted more than just the next matrix—“also the one after that, and the one after that, and the one after that,” he said. Typically, someone solving this kind of problem would be transparent about the methods used to get there; for years, mathematicians have been sharing their work freely on the open-access website arxiv.org. Such is not the M.O. of the A.I. companies. Anthropic did not release logs showing how the solutions were reached. Williamson said that he felt as if an entire garden of mathematics had been killed. “It was the nightmare scenario, like, ‘Here’s the answer, it’s forty-two.’ ”

paragraphs.text: It was less than a month later that OpenAI made its Navier-Stokes announcement. The day before, Tristan Buckmaster, a professor at N.Y.U., posted a statement saying that he and Alpöge, working with the assistance of A.I., had made significant progress toward a solution. OpenAI, which spent millions of dollars’ worth of compute to get there first, said that it had taken less than a week. In Buckmaster’s statement, he voiced concern that OpenAI had accessed his work (he and Alpöge had used OpenAI’s public Codex model, among other L.L.M.s), which the company denied. According to Buckmaster, Sébastien Bubeck, the head of the team at OpenAI that was behind the solution, had offered him authorship of their paper, on the condition that he agree not to include Alpöge. Buckmaster said no. When he threatened to make his interaction with OpenAI public, Bubeck apparently responded by asking, “Why would you ruin your career?”

In Buckmaster’s statement, he voiced concern that OpenAI had accessed his work (he and Alpöge had used OpenAI’s public Codex model, among other L.L.M.s), which the company denied.

According to Buckmaster, Sébastien Bubeck, the head of the team at OpenAI that was behind the solution, had offered him authorship of their paper, on the condition that he agree not to include Alpöge.
Buckmaster said no. When he threatened to make his interaction with OpenAI public, Bubeck apparently responded by asking, “Why would you ruin your career?”

It’s a letter that reflects what was already a reality six months ago.”

paragraphs.text: Socrates is said to have worried that writing would ruin our memories—and Socrates’ crowd probably did remember longer stretches of the Odyssey than any of us do. But the Fields letter argued that the use of A.I. was not like merely off-loading the memorization of poems or phone numbers; it was more like off-loading, or bypassing, daydreaming and debating and thinking. It’s not that humans will come to know too much too quickly but that they will understand less and less—eventually less than we understand now. “The most precious resources of our profession are students and ideas, and these we nurture with great care,” the letter said. Mathematics is a living discipline and an oral tradition, not just a written one. The symbol of the working mathematician is a chalkboard, representing knowledge that can be erased after it’s understood because it is now in the mind.

paragraphs.text: Fefferman, like Tao, was a child prodigy, an early winner of the Fields Medal, and a professor of mathematics by his early twenties. He is now seventy-seven. I asked him how he would describe what working on a math problem feels like. He told me that he had sometimes described it to non-mathematicians as playing chess with the Devil, “but you get to take back moves.” The Devil is a much better chess player—“he crushes you again and again.” But then you go back to the beginning. You experiment with different approaches. You’re still crushed and don’t understand why. “But eventually you hit on something,” Fefferman said. “The whole time, there’s this angel whispering in your ear things like ‘No, no, pin his bishop!’ ” Initially, the angel’s voice is too quiet to make out, but it gets louder. “And your ears get better.” Until, finally, you win one match. And then you’re back at the beginning. “That’s something I love about being a mathematician,” Fefferman said. “If you have a thousand dumb ideas and one really good one, you’re a good mathematician. And that’s not true in many walks of life.”

paragraphs.text: Like everyone I spoke to, Fefferman said that no one knows, really, what will happen to mathematics. He sees both pessimistic and optimistic scenarios, and he suspects that the future will consist of a bit of each. In an optimistic scenario, he can envision A.I. broadening the kinds of questions that can be asked. He explained that sometimes you have a line of thinking that feels like it has only a five-per-cent chance of working out. You might say, “I don’t want to think about this, since it will take me a lifetime to find out.” “That’s different from ‘O.K., it has a five-per-cent chance of working, and it will take me two days to find out,’ ” Fefferman said. “I think people will become more courageous and more imaginative and be freed.” He said that mathematicians used to need both originality and technical power; he had known a very original mathematician who got lost teaching a freshman course. “I think that A.I. will take over power,” Fefferman said. “It’s natural for us mathematicians to feel anxiety. But I think there’s a chance that A.I. will be a great accelerator of progress, and it will be our job to adjust to the new way of doing math.”

paragraphs.text: A deep problem in what is called Gaussian elimination has captivated Urschel for years. During the course of a decade, he developed a research protocol that he was confident could solve it—eventually. But, as A.I.-assisted solutions to Erdős problems started going up online, he worried that he was running out of time. “So I began to rush ahead,” he said. “I had a postdoc, Rikhav Shah, helping me.” Within a week, Shah told Urschel that “he had heard rumors that compute power was being thrown behind problems in Gaussian elimination,” and Shah thought that they should consider using A.I. Urschel agreed. “So I paid the two hundred dollars a month or whatever,” he said, and they worked with GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Fable 5.

paragraphs.text: Urschel walked me through the collaboration with A.I. “So first I asked it, ‘Can you solve this?’ And it said no, and also that it didn’t think what I was telling it was even true,” he recalled. “I said, ‘O.K., here’s this object that has these properties that you didn’t believe existed.’ ” He went on to feed it steps from his research program. The “conversation” went back and forth, with Urschel pushing the A.I. along the axis of his research program, and the A.I. responding in an irksome, sycophantic tone. Urschel directed it to change its tone to be straightforward and honest. Eventually, something “popped out” that was correct but “very, very ugly.”

paragraphs.text: Erdős described proofs that are particularly concise and beautiful—proofs that give you deep insight—as “straight from the Book,” by which he meant the Book of God, though he doubted the existence of God, whom he called the S.F., for Supreme Fascist. Erdős’s first mathematical publication, at age nineteen, was a proof of Chebyshev’s theorem on prime numbers, which had already been proved. But Erdős produced a much simpler proof, one that was succinct and revelatory. A.I. proofs (at least for now) tend to be nothing like straight-from-the-Book proofs. When Urschel looked at the A.I.-assisted proof, he said, “I thought, O.K., we can take this thing and with human work change it into this nice and intuitive thing.” Urschel and Shah published their research, including a detailed endnote of which steps in the process were exclusively human-produced and which were assisted by A.I.

paragraphs.text: Urschel’s program of research had brought about novel, important work. Shah would have a substantive publication behind him when seeking jobs. But Urschel did not feel celebratory. “Let me be clear. There was no fun in this for me,” he said. “The fun was had before I gave it to this computer program. But talking to the A.I. about it—this is not fun.” He recalled, as a kid, falling in love with logic puzzles. What he loved was being in the dark, trying to find his way forward. “The fun part was not understanding, and struggling to understand,” he said. “Having all the solutions written down is the least fun part.”

paragraphs.text: Mathematics “has been living a bit of a double life,” he suggested, and the pressure from A.I. was making that visible. To people outside the discipline, the story is that math is important and that, even at its most abstract, it often ends up leading to all sorts of unexpected applications, like public-key cryptography and G.P.S. “This is the story one tells when one wants grant money,” Urschel said. “But this story is not true. And it has never been true.” Or, at least, it’s mostly not true. Urschel postulated that every mathematician sees himself as being somewhere on a spectrum between scientist and artist. “I would say what I call the more scientist approach is being focussed on trying to push the frontier of things as far as we can as quickly as we can,” he told me. “And the artist perspective is, Let me do something beautiful and enjoyable and manipulate these things, and the act of doing this is really, you know, a joyful thing.”

paragraphs.text: Tao also told me that the narrative of math as having practical importance was a half-truth, at best. Some of his own research has led to cheaper, faster MRI imaging; most of it has been about curiosity, wonder, and play. He told me a story about the mathematician John Conway, whom he knew at Princeton and whose office was crowded with what were, in essence, puzzles and toys. “I remember once he wanted to learn how to see things in four dimensions,” Tao said. “He reasoned that, since our eyes can really only see in two dimensions”—it’s the distance between the eyes that produces parallax and lets us see as if our vision were three-dimensional—“he invented this weird periscope thing, a goggle thing with mirrors, so that the parallax would not just be horizontal but also vertical. He thought this would give him a way to visualize in four dimensions.” Conway built the device and walked around in it, looking like a mad scientist. “But he said the only thing that it ever gave him was a headache,” Tao told me.

paragraphs.text: Tao never solved the problem that Erdős shared with him in 1985. That was done by Hoi Nguyen and Van Vu, in 2010. But Tao did solve a different famous Erdős problem, one that had been formulated around 1930, known as the Erdős discrepancy problem. It was one of the Hungarian mathematician’s favorite problems. He is said to have brought it up often, especially toward the end of his life. It can be thought of as a question about a series of coin flips, continuing on infinitely, and whether that series inevitably becomes “unbalanced” if you look at every second, or third, or any-number-distance entry in it. Another mathematician, James Grime, made the problem more accessible by translating it into a puzzle narrative, involving someone held captive between angry snakes in front of them and a precipitous cliff behind them. The coin flips are steps forward or back, and the question is whether it is possible to survive. You could Google the answer. Or you could play around with the problem first.

chapters.title: Did the World Just Gain Hundreds of Millions of Alzheimer’s Patients?
chapters.subtitle: A new definition of Alzheimer’s includes people without symptoms. Experts are fiercely divided over whether that makes sense—and whether the new drugs really help.

paragraphs.text: Many have heralded a golden age of Alzheimer’s research, excited by the promise of new amyloid-targeting antibodies. Yet a large meta-study of such antibodies concluded that they probably result in “little to no difference” in the decline of memory and of cognitive ability.Illustration by Daniel Liévano

paragraphs.text: This July, some ten thousand people descended on London for the Alzheimer’s Association International Conference. Another three thousand of us joined virtually. I’m an anthropologist, accustomed to conferences where croissants at coffee breaks count as a luxury. This one opened with six trumpeters dressed as Buckingham Palace guards, followed by dancers who discoed, vogued, and high-kicked through the history of British pop. After the first day’s sessions, participants dispersed to parties; at one, singers in sequins belted out covers while someone played an illuminated, transparent violin. One night, the London Eye was lit purple to honor the people in attendance.

paragraphs.text: That optimism followed decades of disappointment. Between 1974 and 2020, the U.S. government spent roughly twenty billion dollars on Alzheimer’s research without seeing the approval of a single treatment designed to act on the disease’s underlying biology, let alone stop or reverse its course. Today, Alzheimer’s afflicts roughly one in nine Americans over sixty-five and, along with related dementias, has been estimated to cost the economy about three-quarters of a trillion dollars a year. In surveys, it ranks with cancer as the disease people fear most.

paragraphs.text: That’s understandable. Alzheimer’s dismantles the self by degrees. It typically starts by robbing patients of recent memories—conversations they just had, where they put important objects—before corroding the basic functions of adult independence, from paying bills to managing medications. Eventually, it leaves patients unable to speak, move, swallow, or recognize close relatives. “We estimate a man by how much he remembers,” Ralph Waldo Emerson wrote, about a decade before an Alzheimer’s-like dementia left him scarcely able to write his name.

paragraphs.text: These high hopes rest largely on two developments. First: drugs. Since 2021, the Food and Drug Administration has approved three antibody treatments meant to slow the disease’s progression. All target amyloid, a protein fragment that can accumulate into the plaques that have long been associated with Alzheimer’s and that many researchers believe plays an important role in its development. Two drugs—lecanemab, sold as Leqembi, and donanemab, sold as Kisunla—are on the market and are covered by Medicare.

paragraphs.text: The second development concerns diagnosis. Until recently, measuring amyloid levels in living patients required expensive PET scans or invasive spinal taps. Blood tests developed over the past five years approach the accuracy of those methods. The F.D.A. cleared the first such test in May, 2025; three more have followed. “For the first time,” Gates wrote, “we have simple blood tests that tell you whether you have Alzheimer’s.”

The result has been to give new urgency to one of the most fiercely debated questions in contemporary medicine: What, exactly, is Alzheimer’s disease?

paragraphs.text: At Donald Kewman’s home, outside Sacramento, there’s a sticker that reads “ALL ARE WELCOME” beside the front door. Inside, the living room shows signs of having been colonized by grandchildren. Bookshelves and a Persian-style rug share space with toy trucks, a purple plastic kitchen, and an easel with a basketball hoop attached to its back. paragraphs.text: Deter never left the asylum. Her speech deteriorated into shouts and hums and eventually almost disappeared. She died in 1906, roughly five years after Alzheimer first saw her. By then, he had moved to Munich, but he had her brain sent to him. Examining it, he detected three abnormalities: deposits of a substance, later identified as amyloid beta; tangles of fibrils inside neurons, now known to be composed largely of tau proteins; and a reduced number of neurons. paragraphs.text: At the time, however, Alzheimer’s disease did not mean what it does today. When Emil Kraepelin, Alzheimer’s supervisor, named the condition in the 1910 edition of his influential psychiatry textbook, he conjectured that it differed from dementia, then the catchall term for cognitive decline in old age. Although Kraepelin recognized that plaques, tangles, and neuronal loss could also occur in the ordinary dementia of old age, he noted that Alzheimer’s patients were unusually young, sometimes in their forties or fifties, and that their illness could take an especially severe course. For much of the twentieth century, “Alzheimer’s disease” was therefore virtually synonymous with “presenile dementia.”

paragraphs.text: It was not until the nineteen-seventies, more than sixty years after Kraepelin named Alzheimer’s disease, that it came to encompass late-onset dementia. The figure most responsible for this was Robert Katzman, a reserved, soft-spoken neurologist who chaired the department at the Albert Einstein College of Medicine, in the Bronx. In the nineteen-sixties, his mother-in-law developed confusion and memory problems. She was sixty-four—just below the conventional cutoff for senile dementia—and so she was diagnosed with “presenile dementia,” or Alzheimer’s disease. The line struck Katzman as suspiciously arbitrary. “It became obvious that Alzheimer’s disease was a single entity regardless of age of onset,” he later recalled.

paragraphs.text: Medicine had a powerful model for deciding that apparently different illnesses were really one disease: identify a common cause. In the nineteenth century, the physician Robert Koch showed that pulmonary consumption, intestinal disease, and swollen lymph nodes could all result from the same bacterium, Mycobacterium tuberculosis. In a two-page editorial published in 1976, Katzman argued that some instances of early- and late-onset dementia should be grouped together as Alzheimer’s disease. His evidence was chiefly descriptive. Both could involve plaques and tangles. He could not show that a single causal process produced both conditions, as Koch had done with tuberculosis. But the shared features, he maintained, were enough.

paragraphs.text: The consequences were enormous. A condition once considered rare now encompassed most forms of old-age dementia. Katzman himself came to regard the editorial as the most important paper he had written. The shift was institutional as well as scientific. In 1974, Congress had created the National Institute on Aging, as part of the National Institutes of Health, but it had struggled for attention. Aging was diffuse and abstract, a difficult cause around which to mobilize resources, in the manner of Richard Nixon’s War on Cancer. But Katzman’s enlarged conception of Alzheimer’s provided a similarly compelling foe. In the opening paragraph of his 1976 editorial, he described the disease as a societal “malignancy” that ranked among the country’s leading causes of death. “We had to make it a household word,” Robert Butler, the first director of the National Institute on Aging, recalled, because funding didn’t flow toward vague biological processes. “People don’t die from basic research, they don’t suffer from basic research. They suffer from specific diseases.”

(A spokesperson for the F.D.A. said that the team’s participation was typical of similar meetings.) Sperling, the Harvard neurologist, told me that separating the world into amyloid-positive and amyloid-negative people is “simplistic.” She, too, thinks risk depends on tau, vascular disease, and other factors, including the amount of amyloid in brain tissues. She acknowledges that researchers still cannot explain why some people accumulate substantial amyloid without developing dementia. Their strongest objection was that pooling antibodies that effectively cleared amyloid with ones that didn’t could obscure the benefits of the newer treatments.

paragraphs.text: The Cochrane authors and their Alzheimer’s Association critics also differed in their ties to the companies whose drugs were being assessed. None of the eleven Cochrane authors reported a relevant financial conflict. Of the thirty-seven authors of the rebuttal, six were employees of the Alzheimer’s Association, and nearly two-thirds disclosed recent relationships with Biogen, Eisai, or Lilly.

paragraphs.text: Richard pointed out that another amyloid-targeting antibody, solanezumab, had already been tested in cognitively normal, amyloid-positive people. In a large trial led by Sperling, the drug slowed amyloid accumulation by about forty per cent and yet showed no evidence of slowing cognitive decline. Solanezumab was, as Richard acknowledged, not the most effective at removing amyloid; in theory, a more potent amyloid-clearer might have fared differently. But the result, published in 2023, was a disappointment for enthusiasts of early intervention. Richard objected to the habit of describing such trials as “failed.” He observed, “These trials have not failed. These are very rigorously conducted, successful clinical trials. But they show a null effect, and it is equally important in science as a positive effect.”

paragraphs.text: Carrillo and others at the Alzheimer’s Association regard the major role of amyloid in Alzheimer’s as essentially confirmed, but a number of researchers wonder whether it confuses an effect with a cause. Some disease models depict amyloid accumulation as downstream of failures in the cellular machinery that processes and recycles proteins. Other scientists argue that vascular dysfunction hinders the brain’s ability to clear amyloid and injures neurons through other routes. In such accounts, removing the deposits may be like battling a fire by clearing the smoke.

paragraphs.text: Alzheimer’s might be better understood as a syndrome, several researchers I spoke with suggested; they saw a pattern of impairment arising from more than one biological process. The rare inherited forms differ importantly from the usual late-onset disease. The distribution of damage, the pace of decline, and even the molecular structure of amyloid filaments can vary. A therapy effective in one case may do little in another. Kewman, who has spent years reading about the disease that may determine his future, was sympathetic to this view. “There are many pathways to Alzheimer’s,” he told me. “I don’t think it’s a unitary disease.”

paragraphs.text: The prospect of Alzheimer’s has, in any case, already led Kewman to reorganize his life. He and Sandy have visited memory-care facilities, trying to imagine what they might someday need. He drinks less, goes to the gym three times a week, and makes a point of staying socially engaged. He’s a volunteer for the Alzheimer’s Association, and he advocates for more research funding and broader access to testing and treatment. He is, as he puts it, “the unusual person” in those advocacy spaces, being neither a caregiver nor someone in cognitive decline but an asymptomatic man whose genes and biomarkers have placed him inside the expanding boundaries of the disease.

paragraphs.text: Earlier this year, he went so far as to write his own obituary, or “memorial minute,” as Quakers call it. It recounts his birth in San Francisco and adoption as an infant; his early love of nature; his career as a psychologist. It describes Sandy and their two sons; the discovery of his biological family and, later, of his genetic risk for Alzheimer’s; his years in clinical trials. It ends with his becoming “Opa” to five grandchildren, “the frosting on his cake of life.”

chapters.title: Common Scams to Avoid

paragraphs.text: Fake-Grandpa ScamThe doorbell rings, and a man who claims to be your grandpa is standing there. He says that you invited him to dinner. He’s holding a box of candy. He looks and smells like your grandpa, but something seems “off.” Grab the candy and yell, “Nice try, Gramps!,” and slam the door. If he keeps ringing the doorbell, call the police. Later, you remember that you did invite him to dinner, but, still, it was probably a scam.

He’s getting a divorce, and spends two hours telling you how he doesn’t know what he’s going to do. Is there any way you can get those two hours back? You can try, but you’re probably out of luck.

paragraphs.text: Tennis-Ball ScamYou take your dog to the park and get out a tennis ball. Your dog jumps up and down, urging you to throw the ball. Against your better instincts, you throw the ball—and immediately realize you’ve been scammed. Even if the dog brings the ball back, it’s just a setup to scam you again and again. Dogs often prey on old people and single people, because they know they’re lonely. Instead of getting a dog, get a teen-ager, as the teen-ager will not get excited by the ball and doesn’t care if you throw it or not.

paragraphs.text: The C-section had been in the cards since their twenty-four-week appointment, but the preeclampsia had been a surprise—or a surprise to him, at least. His wife had been insisting for months that she knew, that she felt, something was going to go sideways. She was full of such premonitions. The worst thing about them was that she only ever remembered the ones that bore out, and failed to recall the significantly more numerous ones that did not. An hour or so before the C-section, in a lull between visits from the surgical team, she’d had another one. She had grabbed his arm and said, “Something bad is going to happen.”

paragraphs.text: It was nearly dawn when he pulled off the freeway toward the veterinary clinic. The dog’s teeth began chattering. He tried to relax so that the dog wouldn’t smell the doom on him, but all he could think about was the distance between where he was and where he needed to be. His wife had probably called the police by now. Had likely started calling hospitals, shouting his name and description over the baby’s guttering wails, into the ears of phone operators and receptionists all over town. Had she found the time to eat something? To pee, to shower? Was she remembering to use the nipple everter? Overhead, the trees were turning pale green with morning light. Around the next bend, the cursed driveway to the veterinary clinic opened up out of nowhere to his right. He kept going. Mostly to confuse the dog but also to give himself courage. He took the next right and went all the way around the block. Then he did it again. The dog pressed his nose against the glass, keening whenever the driveway whooshed by.

In puppyhood, he had held this beloved, preposterous animal on his chest, just as he now held their daughter, and waltzed around the room with him, humming “Moon River” until the warm little body went limp. If he could just let go of that, the dog’s journey could end here. He could run off into the woods, taking the suspect contents of his cerebrospinal fluid with him. chapters.title: The Telephone’s Tangled History of Intimacy and Control
chapters.subtitle: How an invention that brought distant voices close rewrote the rules of conversation and raised an unsettling question: Who else might be listening?

paragraphs.text: It can be be hard to forget that, when we place a call, there might always be someone else listening. From the beginning, the wires have been tapped by what James Gleick calls a range of “invisible interlopers.”Illustration by Rob En Robin

paragraphs.text: On May 25, 1943, millions of Americans sat down by the radio to hear a woman die. They didn’t yet know this, or not exactly. All they’d been told by CBS was that the evening’s episode of the drama series “Suspense” would revolve, unusually, around a single voice: that of the actress Agnes Moorehead. At 6:30 P.M. Pacific War Time, the broadcast began. Over suitably gothic chimes, the show’s host introduced “a new study in terror.” The episode’s writer was Lucille Fletcher, its running time was thirty minutes, and its title was “Sorry, Wrong Number.” Its atmosphere was somehow both frenzied and constrained. Mrs. Stevenson (Moorehead), a neurotic confined to bed, waits for her husband to come home. She tries to call his office, in New York—“Murray Hill 7-0093”—to urge him to hurry up, but, owing to some glitch, when the call connects she overhears two men planning a murder. In the course of another sixteen calls, she tries to get hold of her spouse, the police, and a local nurse, all to no avail. The lines seem constantly busy, and the operators incompetent. Mrs. Stevenson screams with rage—and then fear, because she gradually realizes, as you may have already, that she is the victim-to-be.

paragraphs.text: The victim is also you. One of the sinister appeals of “Sorry, Wrong Number”—which was praised by Orson Welles, a “Suspense” regular, as “the greatest single radio script ever written”—is that it makes us newly conscious of the menace lurking in an everyday technology: the telephone. For, as Mrs. Stevenson grows distressed, you become uncomfortably aware of her physical circumstance. Even as she casts her voice many miles away, she’s trapped. Her telephone’s wires have come to constitute the limits of her world. They’re also the limits of your world, you come to see, whenever you place a call yourself. What you know about the people on the other end of the line—their faces, their postures; whom they’re with, where they are, how truthful they’re being—can stretch only as far as what you’re told and what you choose to believe. Beyond that, you’re making inferences in the dark.
sentences: The victim is also you.

One of the sinister appeals of “Sorry, Wrong Number”—which was praised by Orson Welles, a “Suspense” regular, as “the greatest single radio script ever written”—is that it makes us newly conscious of the menace lurking in an everyday technology: the telephone.
For, as Mrs. Stevenson grows distressed, you become uncomfortably aware of her physical circumstance.
Even as she casts her voice many miles away, she’s trapped.
Her telephone’s wires have come to constitute the limits of her world.
They’re also the limits of your world, you come to see, whenever you place a call yourself.

What you know about the people on the other end of the line—their faces, their postures; whom they’re with, where they are, how truthful they’re being—can stretch only as far as what you’re told and what you choose to believe.
Beyond that, you’re making inferences in the dark.

paragraphs.text: This may strike you as a little paranoid. The rise of the telephone, in the past century and a half—from the rotary diallers at home and the boxes in the street to the smartphones in every pocket—is associated with a change that, broadly speaking, we consider positive. The telephone gave us back what distance had always stolen: the intimacy of voice. Now your parent or your friend or your lover could be a thousand miles away yet softly in your ear. Such was the promise made to America by A.T. & T., a.k.a Ma Bell, the behemoth that, from the turn of the twentieth century to the nineteen-eighties, ran most of the phone industry. Telephones, it declared, were a milestone for us all. One of the company’s advertisements, from 1909, called them tools of “civilization . . . one of the most powerful influences for broadening human intelligence.” By the time of my own childhood, in Britain, a century later, the upbeat mantras hadn’t changed. Nokia: “Connecting People.” T-Mobile: “Life’s for Sharing.” We surely want connection, and we surely want to share. In “The Telephone: A New History” (Farrar, Straus & Giroux), James Gleick begins in agreement, describing his subject as “an ordinary necessity” that has been “essential in the development of modern life.” It would be churlish to say that he’s wrong, or that the big carriers didn’t deliver on part of what they sold. Today, I live in London, a city where I have no family, but, at the touch of a screen, I can talk to loved ones far and wide.

paragraphs.text: Yet that partial intimacy can be unsettling. The telephone seems to abolish distance, but the voice remains fundamentally physical, air percussed by flesh. The telephone is a conjurer: hearing someone speak, we imagine that person with us in the room. Deprived of body language, unable to gauge the person’s tone against the way they touch their cheek or tilt their head, we invent what we cannot see, and may find ourselves wondering how much of our interlocutor is our own creation. The connection itself isn’t entirely under our control. The system we have to use, those wires pulsing with current—or, today, the cell towers humming with signals—belongs to other parties, faceless corporations, themselves possibly under bigger thumbs. It can be hard to forget that, when we route our words through those matrices, there may be someone else listening: since their inception, the wires have been tapped by operators, by eavesdroppers, by what Gleick calls a range of “invisible interlopers.” So we talk blindly into the receiver, and we’re never quite sure of where or how our words will land. “Sorry, Wrong Number” shows the telephone in one of its less examined aspects, as a paranoia machine; but then, as Mrs. Stevenson learned too late, some paranoias are justified.

paragraphs.text: Alexander Graham Bell came, as it were, at the end of a line. His grandfather, Alexander Bell, born in Scotland in 1790, had started off as an actor, then moved into teaching elocution. He worked on stammers and other speech impediments, first in his home town, St. Andrews, then in the great metropole of London. His son, Alexander Melville Bell, born in 1819, went into the same profession, made a great success of it, and wrote popular manuals, including “The Science of Speech” and “Bell’s Standard Elocutionist.” By the late nineteenth century, the name Bell and the practice of elocution—the professional enhancement of the voice—had become close to synonymous. (Decades later, Melville Bell would be one of George Bernard Shaw’s inspirations for Henry Higgins, the phonetics professor in “Pygmalion”; Higgins transcribes Eliza’s pre-tutored voice in Melville’s notation system, Bell’s Visible Speech.)

paragraphs.text: Alexander, or Aleck, son of Alexander Melville, was born in Edinburgh in 1847. After his brothers died young, of tuberculosis, the family quit Britain for Canada, hoping to save their remaining boy. They did, and though Alexander, who added the “Graham” on his eleventh birthday, was rarely in great health, he lived to seventy-five—well beyond the average Victorian. In 1871, he moved to Boston to teach at the Horace Mann School for the Deaf, and soon, at the age of twenty-six, he became a professor at the newly founded School of Oratory. Already fascinated by human voices and other physical phenomena, he examined devices that played with waveforms, vibrations, and sounds. He toyed, in turn, with inventions of his own. In search of help, he visited a local electrical workshop, where he met Thomas Watson, another bright young thing. The two hit it off and began tinkering together above the shop.

paragraphs.text: In due course, with Watson’s aid, Bell invented the telephone, or so many a schoolchild could tell you. It’s true that, on March 7, 1876, he received a U.S. patent that declared it so, giving him the exclusive right to manufacture and sell the telephone, and assuring the Bell System’s rise to preëminence. But, as Gleick reminds us, inventions rarely emerge from a single mind. By 1860, for instance, the German physicist Johann Philipp Reis had invented what he named the Telephon, two devices linked by an electrified wire. Sixteen years later, on the same day that Bell filed for a patent, the electrical engineer Elisha Gray filed paperwork with the patent office as well. Thomas Edison wasn’t far behind, either; and so the queue went on. After the various claims were brought to a head before the Supreme Court, in a struggle so vicious that it may have caused the Chief Justice’s premature death, the Court in 1888 upheld Patent 174,465—and that was that. Bell had invented the telephone, and off it went, expanding in skeins across the land.

paragraphs.text: Gleick has a rich supply of oddities and delights from the telephone’s early history. Just a year after the patent was granted, we learn, America gained its first switchboard, a rickety thing run from a Hartford drugstore. Mark Twain, living nearby, installed a telephone line that he said was “the first one that was ever used in a private house.” (Like many of his claims, this was almost true.) The following year, a commercial exchange opened in New Haven, forty miles south. Six years later, the figures had leaped: Scientific American reported nine hundred and six exchanges and 123,625 American telephone subscribers. (Gleick’s interest, and mine, lies in the telephone’s essential form—sightless conversation at a distance—but carrying the story to the present reveals a world where even Ma Bell and her core technology look modest. Witness the ubiquity of the smartphones on which we so expensively spend our lives.)

paragraphs.text: As the telephone proliferated, it began to remake the social rules. It wasn’t clear, initially, how you ought to behave on it. Even beginning a call was fraught. Then as now, when you met someone in the street, you might greet them with a handshake, a bow, or a kiss, along with some less demonstrative signalling, such as a distance kept or closed, and a few introductory words, such as a formulaic greeting, or an offhand quip, or the thing you’d been longing to say for weeks. The telephone scrambled these habits. It wasn’t just that you and your interlocutor couldn’t see each other; because the earliest phones were always “on,” your opening words had to grab attention. Bell preferred the nautical word “Ahoy,” which was sometimes “Ahoy-hoy,” presumably for the less alert, and, in our own time, for the ancient Mr. Burns of “The Simpsons.” Edison liked “Hello,” also known as “Hallo” or “Hullo” or “Hulloa.” That was an early-nineteenth-century coinage, used for hailing a fellow from afar. Through a mixture of corporate encouragement and popular acceptance, it quickly became the norm. Other injunctions were ignored. The New Haven telephone company, in its early years, encouraged its users to end a conversation by declaring, “That is all.”

paragraphs.text: The telephone could also upend the norms of civility. In 1905, the magazine Telephony cautioned readers against the “hasty communication of tempestuous thoughts to the telephone girl.” Abusing the operator was apparently part of an epidemic of telephone behavior that Telephony deemed “the great ethical problem” of the day. During the same period, a Michigan telephone company offered subscribers bland advice—don’t hog the lines, don’t eavesdrop—but also warned that something deeper was at stake: “Some people take advantage of the telephone to say things to others they would not think of saying were they face to face with them. This shows a cowardly spirit.” More than a century later, such behavior remains familiar. In this light, the telephone seems less like A.T. & T.’s beacon of civilization than like a strong intoxicant.

paragraphs.text: Controlling access to the telephone proved easier than controlling the speech it conveyed. Ma Bell aggressively enforced her patents and granted her subsidiary, Western Electric, exclusive license to make telephone equipment. By the mid-eighteen-nineties, Bell’s original patents began expiring, allowing independent telephone companies to spring up, but A.T. & T.’s infrastructure was already so widespread that denying competitors access to its network could freeze them out of the market. The farther the telephone spread across America, the clearer the problem became. As with the U.S. Post Office, a formal monopoly since the late eighteenth century, Americans rarely had a meaningful way to take their business elsewhere and so push to improve their telephone service. And, though Congress at least set postal rates, A.T. & T. initially charged whatever it liked. Bell’s first telephone sets, which he rented out to users in 1877, were priced according to purpose: twenty dollars a year (six hundred and thirty dollars today) for “social” use and twice that for “business.” By 1894, the average subscription in Manhattan cost two hundred and forty dollars (more than nine thousand dollars today). Not signing up cost both nothing and everything: an advertisement in the early nineteen-hundreds warned reluctant readers that “every new telephone makes you the more isolated.”

paragraphs.text: Such slogans hinted at extortion, and onlookers were unimpressed. As early as 1886, the Times had had enough of the Bell System: “From the beginning it has plundered the people. A fraudulent patent at the foundation, and upon it a business built up by means of stock watering, collusive suits at law, secret alliances with other similar corporations, unjust discrimination and extortionate rates.” That year, some seven hundred subscribers in Rochester, New York, furious at plans to raise their charges, withheld their payments for eighteen months, until the phone company backed down. Then again, perhaps they were lucky to be extorted. Compare Bell, once more, with the Post Office, which was ordered by Congress in 1916 to serve “as nearly as practicable, the entire rural population of the United States.” A.T. & T. was under no such obligation. Theodore Vail, the company’s formidable founding president, spoke airily of “one system, one policy, universal service,” but all he meant by “universal” was the pursuit of monopoly—one nation under Bell. In parts of that nation where service provision would be too costly, A.T. & T. left people literally out of the loop.

paragraphs.text: Some citizens came up with clever work-arounds. Gleick tells us about the “barbed-wire telephone cooperatives” created by farmers on the prairies, who used steel fence wires as cables, one connecting to the next, insulated by corncobs and leather straps. Multiple households shared a circuit, resulting in “party lines,” on which anyone could pick up and join the call. This was a time when the Industrial Workers of the World had a serious foothold in U.S. labor and when sabotage, in the pursuit of workers’ aims, was practiced in rural industries; the farmers’ telephonic moonshine had a similar air of rebellion. Why go begging to Ma Bell when you could rig a contraption of your own? And these measures kept farmers from having their pockets picked in more ways than one: Gleick mentions a cheerful Iowan who, in 1905, declared that, thanks to the barbed-wire lines, “chicken stealing has become a lost art.”

Bell would let smaller companies connect to its long-distance lines and cede control of Western Union, an old rival in which it had bought a controlling stake. In return, Ma Bell would continue to reign.

paragraphs.text: Leviathan, we might recall, was Hobbes’s metaphor for the state. It mediated relations between little guys who’d otherwise hack one another to bits. Such was the authority we deserved. It might also serve as a metaphor for the telephone, not just because the Bell System long enjoyed a stunning monopoly—Gleick brands it “the greatest commercial enterprise the world had ever known”—but because this technology has always involved a third party controlling our two-party links. Originally, this control was open and obvious. Your leviathan was one human and a set of cords. You spoke into your transmitter to an operator at the nearest exchange, gave the number of your desired address, and waited as she plugged and unplugged switchboard jacks, completed circuits, and connected your call. Even after your loved one picked up, the voice of that operator lingered in your ears, as if she were still on the line—which, quite possibly, she was. Reading Gleick’s account of early switching, I came to think that a nineteenth-century time traveller might find nothing unusual about Cold War bugging or N.S.A. wiretapping. The telephone network was never private. Call no line secure until it’s dead.

paragraphs.text: In Hartford and New Haven, the first operators were teen-age boys. As the network expanded, though, the jobs shifted to young women, who became known as Hello Girls. Marcel Proust would rechristen them “Guardian Angels . . . Danaids of the Unseen,” which has more panache. But, as the number of customers soared, manual switching came under strain. By 1910, the New York City area had fifty-two exchanges handling calls to and from three hundred and seventy-six thousand “stations” (likely a telephone or a private switchboard), and the numbers kept climbing. Connecting a call within one exchange took twenty-two seconds, longer for transfers, and, where technology is concerned, impatience springs eternal. How many Danaids of the Unseen could A.T. & T. hope to hire? Still, the company was slow to embrace automatic switching. Operators were cheap and reliable, and, for a long time, executives believed that asking customers to dial numbers themselves was a step backward. Using the telephone was supposed to be effortless.

paragraphs.text: For all its growing pains, the Bell System had become an emblem of American progress. Presidents Wilson and Vail reunited in 1915 to join the first official coast-to-coast telephone call. Bell and Watson, now in their sixties, took their places in New York and San Francisco, respectively, where they reënacted their first exchange, in 1876, with a jokey twist: “Mr. Watson, come here, I want you”; “It would take me a week to get to you this time.” Then Wilson joined the line from the White House, with Vail listening, too, from his Georgia estate. (Gleick writes that Vail had “a silent guest, J. P. Morgan, at his side,” completing the picture of smoky-back-room power, though he means J. P. Morgan, Jr.—the old man had been dead nearly two years—and he could have added that William Rockefeller, Jr., was there as well.) The First World War did cause the telephone industry to be nationalized for a year, but this didn’t make much difference for users, notwithstanding a decree in Indiana that banned speaking German on the phone. (It’s another reminder that no one has ever talked with pure freedom on the telephone: the lines are subject to higher powers.) In April, 1920, Vail died, at the age of seventy-four. For one minute during his funeral, as a mark of respect, all Bell telephone service across America stopped.

paragraphs.text: The Bell System’s growth did not. Automatic switching finally began to spread, first through local exchanges. Rotary phones let users enter numbers themselves, and, at least in American cities, the ability to make local calls by dialling had become commonplace by the nineteen-thirties. Dials also linked numbers to letters, an association that entire nations took to heart. The letters preserved the old exchange names: to call someone on London’s Maida Vale exchange, for instance, you started by dialling 624, corresponding to M-A-I. Gleick mentions Hitchcock’s 1954 film “Dial M for Murder” and its use of a telephone as death’s handmaiden—a cheating housewife is phoned by her husband, who has hired an assassin to hide behind a curtain by the phone—but, when I rewatched the movie recently, I noticed something else. The opening credits show a closeup of a phone and superimpose an “M” on the relevant “MNO” finger hole without showing which number it replaces. A nineteen-fifties viewer would have found this unremarkable, but younger viewers today have no reason to know why “6” equates to “M.”

paragraphs.text: Long-distance calls placed without human assistance started to emerge in mid-century. In 1947, A.T. & T. established a numbering plan with three digits for the area and seven for you. Four years later, customers in Englewood, New Jersey, became the first to dial calls across the country themselves. By the time Hitchcock made his movie, automation had put many of the Danaids of the Unseen out of work, though lots of Americans still waited for “Number, please” well into the nineteen-sixties. Over the following decades, the requests and delays while jacks were fiddled gradually receded. Yet Leviathan endured. By 1960, the country had around forty million telephones, carrying countless American conversations through Ma Bell’s wires. When the system was broken up, in 1984, it had a hundred and fifty billion dollars in assets, nearly a million employees, and, it’s said, enough wire to circle the planet forty-six thousand times.

paragraphs.text: The telephone rearranged social life wherever it spread. If some of those earlier habits seem wonderfully dated now, we might bear in mind that habits often do in retrospect, and ours are likely to go the same way. I think of the nineteen-nineties BBC sitcom “Keeping Up Appearances,” in which Hyacinth Bucket, a middle-class woman with delusions of upward mobility—she pronounces her surname “Bouquet”—boasts of owning a “white slim-line telephone with last-number redial.” She begins a call to her rebellious sister with a warning: “I hope you’re wearing something sensible. . . . It always makes me very nervous to think I might be talking to a miniskirt.” Part of these jokes was on Hyacinth; the rest was on the watching nation, still steeped in etiquette—a mutual surveillance system with its own unspoken force. The telephone merely gave that system new moments in which to exert its power.

paragraphs.text: Little has changed on that front. Think how odd it feels to end a call without saying “goodbye,” yet what need is there to wish that your friends walk with God? (I’ve always liked that Leigh Bowery could end phone calls with “Bored now, bye!”) Technology works on our conventions and behaviors, probing their weak spots, threatening to make them, and us, ridiculous. Yet we become entangled with new inventions—in one sense, unable to live without them; in another, unable to live with them. Whenever you speak to someone, you’re both engaged in a performance, making characters of yourselves, perhaps even a spectacle. The telephone complicates this. It may carry voices, but it makes the absence of their bodies more acute.

paragraphs.text: A magnificent movie that I wish Gleick had mentioned turns on just this truth: “Locke,” a 2014 one-hander of sorts, follows a construction manager, played by Tom Hardy, driving his S.U.V. toward London while making, and taking, a series of painful calls. He tells his wife that a one-night stand with another woman has resulted in a pregnancy; he speaks with his sons, who are waiting for him to come home and watch a soccer match; and, because a huge concrete pour is scheduled for the next morning, he tries to manage the project remotely, talking to his boss, his underling, and others. Eventually, he speaks with the woman from that one-night stand, who’s in the hospital about to give birth to their child. He laughs, pleads, bangs the wheel; like Mrs. Stevenson, he’s pinned in place.

paragraphs.text: One more return to Gleick’s history, and to my favorite of his many arresting facts: Clarence Hickman, an inventor who helped develop the bazooka, also built an early answering machine. The juxtaposition may seem merely cute, but to me, well, it rings too true. Answering machines let you speak to someone who may never answer back. They invite you to talk into silence, to wait and listen. They can devastate you without warning. Reading about Hickman’s prototype, I thought of Jesse Pinkman, in “Breaking Bad.” After his girlfriend dies from an overdose, he lies awake and alone, calling her number again and again, just to hear her voice-mail greeting. Then, one night, the phone company disconnects her line, and, like Eurydice, she’s gone.

paragraphs.text: I thought, too, as Gleick does, of the narrator in Proust’s “Recherche,” who, after his grandmother places a call to him from Paris, realizes that he has never properly listened to her voice: “It was sweet, but also how sad it was . . . fragile by reason of its delicacy it seemed at every moment ready to break, to expire in a pure flow of tears . . . without the mask of her face, I noticed for the first time the sorrows that had scarred it in the course of a lifetime.” He can never see her quite the same way again. And I thought of my own grandmother, who died in 2008. I still remember her eleven-digit telephone number, the pattern that my fingers made on the buttons of my childhood Nokia. I think I remember her voice, too. But it’s been nearly two decades, and I’m not sure I do anymore.

chapters.title: Briefly Noted

paragraphs.text: Music Against the Night, by Yiyun Li (Farrar, Straus & Giroux). The first in a planned trilogy, this richly imagined novel reanimates two historical figures: John Field, the Irish-born pianoforte prodigy and inventor of the nocturne, and Adelaide Percheron, a mixed-race woman born in French India in 1790, whom Field would marry, then discard. The novel begins with Percheron contemplating news of Field’s death, and proceeds to trace their youths, including their meeting, in 1807, when Field is humbled by Percheron’s virtuosity on the piano. The two, Li shows, might have done well to consider the opinion of a minor character: “All this talk of being a prodigy or a genius—these things often lead to misery.”

paragraphs.text: Her Kind, by Sophie Lefens (HarperCollins). This début novel centers on Ada, a young mother marked by abandonments: when she was sixteen, her mother left her, and, at the book’s outset, her husband has just done the same. The split prompts Ada to move, with her eighteen-month-old son, to an aunt’s ramshackle house near Lake Michigan. While there, she is racked with visions of mortal danger, and invites three women friends—a violinist, a struggling painter, and a costume designer—to visit, in order to assess which of them she should ask to care for her son in the event of her death. As Lefens mixes spiritual elements with the quotidian, the novel examines the paradoxes of safety, responsibility, and trust.

paragraphs.text: A World We Share, by Roger Berkowitz (Yale). Hannah Arendt never developed a general theory of friendship, yet the concept, as this study shows, anchors much of her political thought. Combining Arendt’s written reflections with portraits of her relationships, Berkowitz offers a model of mutual understanding for our era of epidemic loneliness and polarization. For Arendt, friendship required only respect, duration, and ongoing conversation; ideological agreement wasn’t necessary, as her own friendships bore out. Her correspondence records heated debates on contentious issues, including Zionism, and it’s these encounters that give the book its force, revealing the effort needed to maintain intimacy across profound differences.

paragraphs.text: The Flying Death, by Matt O’Hara (Farrar, Straus & Giroux). This unsettling pharmacological history is propelled by the story of two men: Richard Gill, an American with multiple sclerosis who became convinced, while living in Ecuador in the nineteen-thirties, that Kichwa plant medicine could heal him and make him rich; and Boris Krukoff, a Russian plant hunter who worked for Big Pharma. Gill and Krukoff separately pushed their way into Indigenous communities, bribing or cajoling elders to forage vines and process toxic plant compounds known as curare. By 1939, American companies discovered that a curare derivative could relax patients’ muscles; they also erroneously believed that the drug could anesthetize. This innovation eventually contributed to a Nobel Prize win. It was also, O’Hara shows, founded on the drugs’ use during operations by doctors who wrongly assumed that their patients could not feel pain.

chapters.title: The Trouble with Saying What You Mean
chapters.subtitle: In “The Channel,” the poet Jana Prikryl borrows voices from Shakespeare and her own past to explore exile, family, and the possibilities of expressing private grief.

paragraphs.text: “While the others spoke,” Jana Prikryl writes, “my meaning was coming through.” That’s how “Chorus,” the first poem in her fourth collection, “The Channel” (Norton), begins. Who are “the others”? Prikryl doesn’t say. Maybe she’s thinking of the nattering media, or other poets, or just the ordinary chorus of voices absorbed in the course of a day, echoing in her head. “You shouldn’t suppose they expressed my views / or even the opposite exactly,” she cautions. Rather, “meaning was elsewhere and I kept it to myself.” But how can you keep meaning to yourself and still write poems for other people to read?

That’s how “Chorus,” the first poem in her fourth collection, “The Channel”
(Norton), begins.
Who are “the others”?
Prikryl doesn’t say.
Maybe she’s thinking of the nattering media, or other poets, or just the ordinary chorus of voices absorbed in the course of a day, echoing in her head.
“You shouldn’t suppose they expressed my views / or even the opposite exactly,” she cautions.
Rather, “meaning was elsewhere and I kept it to myself.”
But how can you keep meaning to yourself and still write poems for other people to read?

paragraphs.text: “Basically I hate poetry that pretends it’s possible to say what you mean,” Prikryl has said in an interview. “For me, the excitement of writing something like a poem usually resides in prodding and questioning the words that claim to represent what my brain claims to want to be saying.” This self-interrogating method makes for a nervy, difficult style. In “The Channel,” Prikryl writes run-on sentences that layer fragmentary clauses, one after another. Her syntax twists this way and that, as if it were squirming to get out of her packed stanzas, before she pulls up short with a joke or breaks off altogether, choosing silence, with new questions floating in the air. A reader might reasonably decide that Prikryl is more interested in keeping meaning to herself than in getting it across. But that would be a mistake.

paragraphs.text: Prikryl’s suspicion of easy self-expression leads her to try on other voices. “The Channel” is full of references to Shakespeare—to “King Lear” in particular, featuring extended monologues by Cordelia and the Fool. (Historically, Cordelia and the Fool could be played by the same actor, and the two truthtellers appear to merge when Lear mourns his daughter at the end of the play, declaring, “My poor fool is hanged.”) These monologues are interspersed with short lyrics in what initially seems to be the poet’s own voice. But the distinction doesn’t hold. From the first, Prikryl mixes her life story into her characters’ speeches, while the autobiographical lyrics begin to feel like dramatic monologues in disguise. In the poem “Cliff Notes,” Cordelia declares, “Backstage I’m scribbling lyric poems / to prove there is a place where I can be.”
