paragraphs.text: The mingling of voices works best when the reader is unsure whether it’s Prikryl or Cordelia speaking, and when they seem to speak together. Imagine that “Chorus” is spoken by Cordelia. Then “the others” would be her monstrous older sisters. Remember how the play starts: Goneril and Regan flatter Lear when he demands that they profess their love for him in exchange for a piece of Britain, whereas Cordelia, refusing the transaction, keeps meaning to herself. “What would I do without them,” the poem ends. If this is Cordelia talking, it is an admission that her strict truth depends on her sisters’ gross blandishments. If we hear it as Prikryl speaking, it is a wry acknowledgment that her style, for all its brio and individuality, is compelled by the poetic clichés she hates and, in that way, owes something to them.

paragraphs.text: In our era of No Kings rallies, the contemporary political relevance of a mad ruler demanding public displays of fealty is so obvious that Prikryl doesn’t need to press the point very hard. Fathers are important in “The Channel,” but Prikryl is less interested in Lear than in Cordelia, the banished favorite, who is known as much for what she doesn’t say as for what she does. She’s something of a missing character in “King Lear”—“an aperture in the story,” as Prikryl puts it. When Lear disowns her, the King of France accepts Cordelia as his wife and takes her back to his homeland. She is offstage for much of the play, returning in the fourth act at the head of a French military expedition to rescue her father and restore his rights. These absences give Prikryl room to imagine what Shakespeare leaves unwritten. With titles like “Dover Calais” and “Calais Dover,” Prikryl’s monologues follow Cordelia back and forth across the English Channel, folding the poet’s own journeys into Cordelia’s. In “Calais Dover,” an army approaches England on a passenger ferry “circa 1992.” “Anachronism makes all this possible,” the speaker observes.

Five years later, her parents fled the Communist state with her and her older brother. The family moved first to Austria and then to Canada. This period was “baffling” to the child, as Prikryl has described it. When her parents told her that they would be going to a new country, she asked, “What is a country?” In “The Channel,” the cognitive and emotional challenge of crossing borders is captured by Cordelia falling into the English Channel—a slapstick flourish that Prikryl adds to the source text. paragraphs.text: Imagining this scene, Prikryl recalls an indelible image from the refugee crisis in Europe: “The two-year-old / left face-down on a beach nine years ago / came up for me.” The border is a zone of peril and potential death, but also a space of personal transformation. Prikryl says that crossing a border into a new life takes “a special kind / of willing. Assertion without basis / in history, sort of like a person.” Leaving one country for another requires an embrace of a life you cannot know in advance. Something similar happens when Prikryl speaks as Cordelia or the Fool. When she takes on another voice, who she is, how she speaks, and what she means change with the crossing.

paragraphs.text: Prikryl’s early dislocations made language feel as fungible to her as national identity. In Austria, German replaced Czech; in Canada, English replaced German. Those shifts may help explain her relish for the oddities and varieties of English. The new collection combines Elizabethan locutions with scientific terms like “siliceous ooze,” “vuggy leavings,” and “coccolithophores,” and sprinkles in French and Czech. “Haiku” is a seven-line poem written entirely in Czech. You can run its unfamiliar letter combinations and diacritical marks through Google Translate, but that’s not the point of the prank. Prikryl wants us to confront the raw-material strangeness of language. For a moment, you’re as baffled as a five-year-old who has just switched countries.

paragraphs.text: In “The Knots,” one of Cordelia’s monologues, Prikryl narrates a visit to her father. Dementia has made Czech more available to him than the English he has spoken fluently for decades. As words fail him, “what’s left is tone / a style, the substance that composes him / unmellowed in the light.” The juxtaposition of Prikryl’s family with Cordelia’s reveals the overlap of tragedy, fairy tale, and soap opera. Some memories are warm, almost cozy, as when Prikryl recalls, “So much television / as a family, I loved all kinds / through their eyes, facing the same way.” But she hardly idealizes her family history. paragraphs.text: “Roy Lichtenstein: Like New” (at the Whitney through May 10th) is a masterpiece of curation and design, an exhibition that positions Lichtenstein as the last happy white man in American art. Organized with esprit and imagination by the artist Alex Da Corte and the curator Meg Onli, it’s the first retrospective of Lichtenstein’s work in New York since his splash at the Guggenheim in 1993. The show takes up the museum’s entire fifth floor and ends as it begins: with the artist’s signature brightly colored brushstrokes, lines, and Benday dots causing pleasurable kinetic movements in the mind. Lichtenstein’s dynamic style is ubiquitous by now—as are his professional sheen and finish—but that doesn’t cancel out his winning charm, which, like most charm, can warm you up or wear you out. At “Like New,” you may experience both feelings. It’s a show that aims to keep the real world, our gothic political climate included, at bay, while also distracting us from what one might call the grief porn of contemporary art and its constant reminders of our failures as humans.

paragraphs.text: For years now, the Whitney has foregrounded race- and gender-based political art, and it’s a little trippy to walk around this show’s pearl-gray-painted rooms, looking at Lichtenstein’s Fantastik-clean white world of orderly studios, shiny blondes, and square-jawed men, in a place where white male power has been repeatedly denounced and the sins of past neglect redressed. No one can make up for the past—certainly not by demanding that it be corrected in the present—and it was perhaps inevitable that the Whitney would have to turn, or return, to white men with name recognition to get people back into its galleries post-COVID. Exhibitions devoted to Jasper Johns and Andy Warhol helped, and still fit the Whitney framework: both artists were queer. And although Lichtenstein wasn’t gay, there’s enough irony about gender in his early work to qualify him as being interestingly gay-adjacent.

paragraphs.text: Still, it’s difficult to entirely undo the way we’ve been viewing art for a while now, and, after having a great time at “Like New,” you may find yourself feeling slightly guilty about it. But one of the more poignant subtexts of the show is that it’s a reminder of the New York avant-garde in the sixties, and of what a beautiful, forceful energy there was to its various voices, with Lichtenstein the least dirty and anarchic of them all. There’s a sweetness in that, and a sadness, too.

paragraphs.text: I first spent time with Lichtenstein’s work in the early eighties, when I took a class at Columbia on the art of the nineteen-sixties. The professor led us from the glory days of Abstract Expressionism in the fifties, through the emergence of Robert Rauschenberg and Johns by the end of that decade, to this new era in American art. Inspired by Marcel Duchamp and his poetry of the everyday, Rauschenberg and Johns used commonplace objects—a flashlight, a bedspread—in their creations. But artists working under the Pop-art banner in the sixties, including Lichtenstein, Claes Oldenburg, James Rosenquist, Tom Wesselmann, Marisol, and Warhol, picked at the surface of the world that had made them, in order to show us how much it could reveal about what lay beneath it. You can still feel, in the memorable work produced during that period, the critical embrace of all those dance-lesson diagrams, Campbell’s soup cans, ice-cream cones, and Coca-Cola bottles, alongside images of electric chairs, car crashes, and atomic-bomb detonations.

paragraphs.text: In the Cold War universe, where everyone was isolated and class was defined by the power to acquire (and to oppress), Pop artists painted or sculpted what they saw and heard. The artist’s “aura” had no place in those works; instead, Pop art was a kind of supersonic whistle heralding the disasters to come, that had already come. But unlike, for instance, Rosenquist, in such charged political pieces as “F-111” (1964-65), which juxtaposes consumer objects with missiles, Lichtenstein made work that was less about conscience than about control, and the eradication of mess, of feeling.

paragraphs.text: Lichtenstein became Lichtenstein in 1961, when he made “Look Mickey.” He had flirted with cartoon characters before then, but “Look Mickey” took things further. Four feet by nearly six, the painting features the brightest of reds, blues, and yellows. In it, Mickey Mouse and the bombastic Donald Duck are standing on a dock, fishing. Mickey covers his laughing mouth because Donald thinks he’s hooked a fish, but the hook is caught on his own coat. The delight of the painting is the pleasure that Lichtenstein took in the joke—and in this new way of making work that was both free and not free of the artist’s hand. (In the age of Pop, achieving an automated look was part of the process.)

paragraphs.text: Decades before Richard Prince made his fantastic and forlorn cartoon paintings, Lichtenstein was already exploring the idea of entertainment and raising questions: If cartoons were a form of entertainment, was painting a cartoon a form of entertainment, too? Was modern art a put-on? Or something that could be put on? One question that the Whitney show didn’t answer for me was how Lichtenstein got to cartoons, and then to his comic-strip paintings, with their speech balloons, women in distress, and silent men—whose reserve makes us wonder if their creator was a silent man, too.

paragraphs.text: Born in 1923, into an upper-middle-class German Jewish family in New York, Lichtenstein grew up on the Upper West Side, with easy access to museums and other cultural institutions. He loved music and art, and in 1940 he enrolled at Ohio State University, where he studied life drawing, painting, and the work of the masters, including Picasso. If he insisted on pursuing art, his parents felt, it would be good for him to get a degree, in case he had to teach to get by.

paragraphs.text: The Whitney retrospective includes “Drawing by Seeing,” a short film about Lichtenstein’s artistic education, made by Da Corte, whose own work includes video, performance, and installations, driven by the kind of avant-gardism that Lichtenstein espoused for a time. The film is shot in color, but with the performers and their costumes colored a “Twilight Zone” gray. It features a voice-over drawn from a text by Hoyt L. Sherman, Lichtenstein’s teacher and mentor at Ohio State. Sherman’s work centered on perception; he’d flash an image on a screen and then have his students draw what they had seen. Or hadn’t. Da Corte’s film also animates some of Lichtenstein’s early works, including “Step-on Can with Leg” (1961), a two-panel painting that shows a woman’s high-heeled foot stepping on the pedal of a closed garbage can, and then the same image with the lid open. Like Warhol, in “Before and After,” a study of a nose job, also from 1961, Lichtenstein was interested in how time can be represented in a static medium, thus changing how we see a thing, or making us realize that we weren’t really looking.

paragraphs.text: Lichtenstein’s studies were interrupted when he was drafted, in 1943, but he returned in 1946 to finish his degree on the G.I. Bill. By 1949, he was married to the artist Isabel Wilson Sarisky, with whom he had two sons. (Divorced in 1965, he married Dorothy Herzka, a philanthropist, in 1968.) Lichtenstein, shy and reclusive, was a responsible fellow; he supported his family by teaching, while making art that was at first representational, then a little abstract, not terribly distinguished. The breakthrough came in 1960, when he was teaching at Douglass College (which later became part of Rutgers), where he met the performance artist Allan Kaprow, who introduced him to Claes Oldenburg and George Segal, artists who were as taken with the look and signs of masculinity as Lichtenstein was. (Oldenburg’s 1959 work “ ‘Empire’ (‘Papa’) Ray Gun,” for instance, plays on the phallic shape of a firearm.) Surely the freedom that Lichtenstein saw in those sculptors’ work and at Kaprow’s “happenings” helped to release him and open him up to his strongest qualities as an artist: his interest in gender and his amused wit.

paragraphs.text: Lichtenstein’s wonderful early work “Masterpiece” (1962) still makes me laugh. In it, a couple are looking at a canvas. The woman, a blonde, has a speech balloon issuing from her red lips: “Why, Brad darling, this painting is a masterpiece! My, soon you’ll have all of New York clamoring for your work!” The man is silent, only partially visible, in profile; the woman is our focus. She may be the kind of woman who needs her man to be a success, in order to validate her power as a woman, one who, unlike Donald Duck, has caught a big one. It’s a joke on the bright and shiny, profit-driven art world, where nothing resonates like success. Among other great early works, there’s the funny, ’tude-filled “Ohhh . . . Alright . . .” (1964)—a closeup of a red-haired woman on the phone, looking slightly annoyed as she speaks the title—and “Drowning Girl” (1963), in which a blue-haired woman with tears falling from her closed eyes drowns as much in misbegotten love as in a swirl of black-and-white waves. A thought bubble reads, “I don’t care! I’d rather sink—than call Brad for help!”

paragraphs.text: These are not really paintings about distress or isolation. They’re about fake feelings in a manufactured world. What was real in Pop? What wasn’t? I liked these works so much when I was younger, and still do, because, for me, Lichtenstein was at his strongest when he wasn’t just a straight man but, rather, a Warhol-adjacent straight man who could critique both masculinity and the self-consciously feminine. The truth is that when Lichtenstein stopped painting “gay,” I stopped looking. From the seventies on, in work that seemed influenced by Léger, Matisse, Picasso, and others, he appeared to be more at play with the straight boys than questioning their performative creativity. (The Whitney curators have put some of the gay back into his work by treating it as a kind of exquisite California-modern decoration; all that’s missing are gray throw pillows.) Still, at the end of the show, I stood by Da Corte’s replica of Lichtenstein’s enormous 1967 work “Super Sunset Billboard,” which shows a horizon and, above it, white streams of light shooting up and out, like klieg lights announcing a show. The painting is the show. Da Corte and Onli have placed the piece in front of a wall of windows overlooking the Hudson; it’s a calming, lovely thing to see a “real” sky echoing Lichtenstein’s. It’s also a thrilling and moving coda to his work—so much so that I got goosebumps. It was the first time I’d ever thought of goosebumps as Benday dots.

chapters.title: A Song of Grief and Union in “Lincoln in the Bardo”
chapters.subtitle: Missy Mazzoli’s operatic adaptation of George Saunders’s novel is a charismatic, openhearted work.

paragraphs.text: The Swedish baritone Peter Mattei stars as Abraham Lincoln mourning his son.Illustration by Daniele Castellano

paragraphs.text: A measure of vitality in opera—or any creative form—is the number of interesting artists it carries into the open space of mid-career. The innovations of early work are frequently flukes. The middle years bring longer strides and deepening ambitions. The sixth opera by the forty-six-year-old American composer Missy Mazzoli premièred, last month, at the Metropolitan Opera, with an air of arrival that seemed leavened by relief. Mazzoli, once best known for her indie-electro band, Victoire, has emerged as one of our leading dramatic composers, and the opera, “Lincoln in the Bardo,” written with her longtime librettist, Royce Vavrek, is both her first Met commission and the company’s first première by a woman. An occasion like that deserves a charismatic, openhearted work, and Mazzoli and Vavrek deliver one in the form of a comedy with a melancholy guise. Based on the novel by George Saunders and set a year into the Civil War, the opera follows Abraham Lincoln as he visits his deceased eleven-year-old, Willie, in the cemetery where the boy lies amid restless ghosts. The President has not resigned himself to the death, and neither has his son.

paragraphs.text: “Bardo” is a Tibetan term, referring to an intermediate state following death, but its assonance with the English “bard”—one who recites, or sings, tales of lives and deeds—can’t have been lost on Saunders. The residents of the graveyard rehash their pasts obsessively, ritualistically, and all the time. In a basic sense, they can’t let go; they linger, fretting about experiences never tasted, errors left unremedied, vindications not received. Their self-absorption is so great that they do not realize they are dead. (They think they’re convalescing.) They refer to their coffins as “sick-boxes” and complain, like captious hostel guests, about the lack of blankets.

paragraphs.text: Opera is a hybrid form, allowing for storytelling approaches not available to the novel. In the early scenes, Mazzoli and Vavrek weave two supporting characters, Vollman and Bevins, into a single aria of aggrievement. Vollman, a homely middle-aged printer (sung by the baritone Ryan McKinny), was on the verge of consummating his marriage when a falling beam killed him. Now he rests in a purgatorial state of sexual excitement, fitted onstage with a buffa penis that disturbingly resembles a piñata. (The appendage, lofted by a valiant puppeteer, is briefly played for laughs and never seen again.) Bevins, sung by the tenor Jonah Hoskins, is a young gay man who slit his wrists after being jilted by a lover. His song is an overwrought lament of curlicues and tortured intervals dancing around Vollman’s squarer line, for an effect both dreamlike and uncanny. Their two complaints—love without sex and sex without love—mark a barycenter of human loss, the stuff of operatic duets.

paragraphs.text: Elsewhere in the Bardo we find three Black people who had lived through slavery and were buried in coffinless graves, and a ghoulish pair of boozy sadists, Mr. and Mrs. Baron, imagined somewhere between the Dickensian and the Dahlian as they teeter in a sick, odd-meter duet. But the heart of this production is the dramatic soprano Christine Goerke, who plays a deceased clergyman known as the Reverend. Goerke is a wonderful actress, funny and free, who can project irony while projecting her voice. The bravura aria that Mazzoli gives her at the start of the second act—soaring and droll, and slowly intensifying—is a musical delight. In another gender-swapped role, the celebrated countertenor Anthony Roth Costanzo plays Miss Elise Traynor, a fourteen-year-old trapped in the Bardo. Her lilting, clucking vocal line may not contribute much to Costanzo’s musical reputation, but the part adds mightily to his repertoire of outré costuming, which includes singing Philip Glass’s “Akhnaten” nude. Miss Traynor—a kind of nightmare version of the Queen of the Night—appears swathed in an enormous, mildewing white dress, its hems nibbled by rubber pig heads. She’s a cautionary tale of what awaits children who “tarry” in this world of irresolution, and the dramatic arc of the opera follows Bevins, Vollman, and the Reverend’s scheme to compel the President and his son to move on.

paragraphs.text: To Lincoln, Willie’s death is weighted with the Civil War. “I have exported this grief / three thousand times,” he laments. When he enters the crypt and embraces his son’s corpse, his shirtfront glows and throbs like a linked Bluetooth device—the way the production, directed with a marvellous contemporary edge by Lileana Blain-Cruz, signals Saunders’s concept of “occupation,” in which ghosts enter living people and their thoughts. The Swedish baritone Peter Mattei, who sings Lincoln, is tall and rightly renowned for his rich, unmuddy voice, here channelled into plausible Midwestern vowels. Yet his aspect onstage, vexed and exercised and diligently in tempo, is nearer in spirit to the Wagnerian mountaintops than to the lonely terrors of a plainsman, and the dazzling performance he delivers ends up seeming less specific than so singular an opera might call for.

paragraphs.text: Mazzoli, who has trained as a death doula, is known for burrowing deep into specific worlds. (For the reputation-making “Breaking the Waves,” based on the Lars von Trier movie, she and Vavrek studied the language and the music of the Scottish Highlands.) In “Lincoln in the Bardo,” she has produced a rich twenty-first-century score with musical shadows of both the Civil War era and the Halloween graveyard, opening with a spooky stacked minor tone cluster (made spookier by knitting needles rattling the percussion) and extending to gorgeous snatches of chocolatey writing in the low brass, befitting a bereaved President. The orchestra, under the direction of Yannick Nézet-Séguin, comes at this music with terrific confidence, delivering the sort of fully conceived performance that rarely awaits brand-new work (and only occasionally overpowering the singers). Mazzoli’s setting of text can be a mixed bag; her melodies now and then seem to take a purgatorial path themselves, patiently cycling among set intervals when the ear, and the libretto, might wish them to move. But the intelligence of her dramatic writing haunts the score. She makes much of big glissandos, in which the men and women of the chorus slide together through a scale, like a winding siren. Heading upward, these slides impart moments of ecstatic, unworldly levitation. Sent downward, they plummet us into the earth.

paragraphs.text: Saunders’s novel mixes his characters’ epitaph-like accounts of their lives and other dialogue with real text from the historical record, blurring the boundary between speech, which rises in living time, and writing, which exists outside it. The page, we are meant to see, is an inherently ghostly place, at once a paltry shadow of the world it describes and a realm of empathetic reach. The written word, like the Bardo, carries both life, in all its specificity and imperfection, and abstractions of the sort that might define a nation, affording people trapped within themselves a chance to step into other points of view. In a climactic effort to enjoin Willie and the President to go on without each other, the spirits—not least Thomas Havens, a Black freedman, movingly sung by the young tenor Joshua Blue—gather in an effort to occupy Lincoln together. Union is the governing metaphor, and, in the book, it’s a union carried by the intermingling of voice and text, of varied experience and inky phrase. “Lincoln in the Bardo,” published in the first weeks of the first Trump Administration, today reads distinctly as a novel of the Obama years.

paragraphs.text: Despite an occasional groan of narrative machinery, Vavrek ably repaces Saunders’s story line and carries its texty voices into song. Gnarled, consonant-laden phrases such as “conjoined, mass-minded, positive intention” and “two passing temporarinesses” are hard to say, let alone sing. They are retained here as if to underscore the messy peculiarity of the world left behind. The language of the afterlife, by contrast, seems flat and stutteringly insistent: “Lingering lingering lingering,” the dead intone. “Worthy worthy worthy.” In one of the opera’s lovelier ensemble arias, the ghosts praise “the things of the world,” enumerating the small, sticky details that they miss from human existence: “beerfroth,” “toweling off one’s clinging shirt post June rain.” Language, like irresolution, is a thing that belongs to the living world.

chapters.title: “Wild Horse Nine” Gets Lost on Easter Island

paragraphs.text: The first time John Malkovich played a killer trained by the C.I.A., he was a man of many disguises, elusive and unpredictable as the wind. The film was “In the Line of Fire” (1993), and his character, nicknamed Booth, was a psychotically disgruntled agency alum, plotting to murder the President with a custom-built plastic gun and a bullet that he stored in a rabbit’s foot. His other weapon was his voice, at once coldly precise and dangerously soft; never before had Malkovich’s distinctly odd cadences sounded so menacing. Booth spent a lot of time on the phone, taunting a veteran Secret Service agent (Clint Eastwood) about his failure, decades earlier, to protect John F. Kennedy. “Late at night, when the demons come, do you see the rifle coming out of that window?” he drawled. “Or do you see Kennedy’s head being blown apart?”

paragraphs.text: That tragedy looms heavily, but also with an air of jokey inconsequence, over “Wild Horse Nine,” a new film written and directed by Martin McDonagh. It begins in 1973, in Santiago, Chile, where Chris Carlisle (Malkovich), a longtime C.I.A. operative, is stationed. Early on, he reminisces about the popularly elected regimes that he’s toppled, from Guatemala to Congo, and—here his voice drops to a low murmur—acknowledges a prominent role in the Kennedy assassination. Yet, despite this dabbling in POTUS-cide, Chris is something of an anti-Booth; he has too much debonair wit, too much bon-vivant style. He and his loyal protégé, Lee Chesterfield (Sam Rockwell), are headed to Easter Island for a week, and Chris, looking dandy in bright-colored neckties and a porkpie hat, has no use for disguises. As for a rabbit’s foot, forget it: Chris’s luck has run out. He’s dying of cancer and has decided that Easter Island will be his last hurrah. He wants Lee, whose marksmanship he trusts as much as his friendship, to hasten his departure.

Whenever McDonagh hits a stale comic patch like this, he retreats swiftly into the trappings of plot: Lee is understandably less than thrilled about Chris’s instant-death wish, but, by all appearances, M.J. (a cranky Steve Buscemi), the C.I.A.’s South American bureau chief, already has a finger on the trigger. Chris, often strung out on morphine, his memory and his wits addled by cancer, has become a jaw-flapping liability.

paragraphs.text: Despite the far-flung setting and the spy-thriller machinations, then, we are in terrain that McDonagh knows all too well: the bloody buddy comedy. Like his film “In Bruges” (2008), “Wild Horse Nine” follows two hit men on holiday, and, like “The Banshees of Inisherin” (2022), it conjures the verdant magic of a remote island setting. Yet the flavor of the proceedings is markedly different. In “Inisherin,” a bitter clash between two friends, played by Colin Farrell and Brendan Gleeson (who both also starred in “In Bruges”), felt exquisitely of a piece with the local elements: the mists, the jagged rocks, the salty tang of the sea. The outdoors lent a wry, soulful grandeur to the characters’ expletive-riddled bickering.

paragraphs.text: There are profanities aplenty in “Wild Horse Nine,” as there are in all McDonagh’s movies and plays. (Cut out the F-bombs and most of them would run barely an hour.) And the vast expanse of Easter Island, majestically filmed by the cinematographer Ben Davis, is astonishing to behold. (Lee himself can’t resist filming with a Super 8 camera, and his grainy images add welcome blips of texture.) Feral horses roam the landscape, and they give the movie both its title and its desired genre: McDonagh strives for the laconic sweep of a classic Western. But not all material can command a space this vast, and I suspect that John Ford himself might have struggled to wring much poetry from Chris and Lee, two ugly-American blowhards wisecracking their way around paradise. Really, the shenanigans could have been transplanted anywhere: picture two guys farting at Stonehenge for an hour or two, only to realize, like the ancients before them, that it makes an awfully nice burial ground.

paragraphs.text: Within such comedic confines, and with a surprising dearth of violent mayhem, “Wild Horse Nine” strains for thematic expansiveness. Ostensibly, the film is about the mixed blessings of friendship, the soul-corroding nature of violence, the horrors of U.S. foreign policy, the possibility of redemption, and the inescapability of death. But it’s the stiffest, least cohesive film on those subjects you could imagine. McDonagh organizes his scenes into thematic blocks, and whenever he loses interest in one block he simply switches, mechanically, to the next. The conversations that he’s written for Chris and Lee toggle between humor and pathos, between self-satisfied snark and self-conscious elegy, and there’s barely a moment when you don’t hear the grinding of tonal gears. (You hear it in the music, too; the Rolling Stones’ “Out of Time” isn’t the subtlest of needle drops.)

paragraphs.text: McDonagh’s dialogue is famed for its staccato crackle, but here he slows the characters’ rhythms, as if to accommodate the diminution of Chris’s body and mind, and packs dead air around everyone’s lines. Yet within those rhythms Malkovich does locate odd, narcotized flashes of poetry. His voice is lower and shakier than usual, and the gleam in his eyes sometimes goes ambiguously dull: are Chris’s mental lapses real, or part of some long con? Chris hasn’t lost his saucy erudition; one of his funnier bits is a mid-breakfast monologue on why “gay countries,” like France, produce the highest-quality cheeses. But he seems on precarious ground, no longer certain of his punch lines. He is also rediscovering the guilt and terror of his Catholic upbringing, and he wonders if, after a life spent overthrowing democracies—the coup that will depose President Salvador Allende is in the offing—he has a chance in hell of entering Heaven.

Chris and Lee refer to them as “the big heads,” and when a tourist couple gently note that the Indigenous term is “moai,” Lee erupts in fury—though Rockwell, who’s good at modulating an explosion, makes clear that Lee is exaggerating his rage for Chris’s benefit. Earlier, at the Santiago airport, they had an awkward run-in with two Chilean college students, Monica (Mariana di Girolamo) and Alicia (Ailín Salas), one of whom explained that the Indigenous name for Easter Island is Rapa Nui. “You shouldn’t even know the word ‘Indigenous’ at your age,” Chris replied.

paragraphs.text: It’s telling that McDonagh hammers the word “Indigenous” repeatedly and contemptuously—as opposed to, say, “local” or “Polynesian.” Back in the seventies, the term was less prevalent in English than it is today, but McDonagh, not for the first time, is eager to mock the language of the contemporary liberal scold. Farrell’s “In Bruges” character wasted no opportunity to call a dwarf a midget; in “Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri” (2017), McDonagh’s most pugnacious and polarizing work, Rockwell played a racist cop, annoyed that “persons of color” had replaced his favorite epithet. You could argue, I suppose, that a film shouldn’t be reduced to its characters’ politics. But, by now, it’s hard to assume that these smug linguistic sensitivities—wielded only, of course, in response to other people’s smug linguistic sensitivities—belong to anyone other than McDonagh himself. And they speak to the narrow view that he takes of his chosen setting and the harrowing historical episode into which he’s seen fit to shoehorn his characters.

paragraphs.text: “Three Billboards” hinged on the racist cop’s reformation, and “Wild Horse Nine,” with less outrageousness and more finesse, undertakes its own dubiously reconstructive exercise. Despite its misanthropic pose, the film wants very badly for us to like and even love Chris, to find him as charming as he is cancel-worthy. Chris regards his role in the deaths and disappearances of thousands of innocents with a weary shrug—and, on rare dark nights of the soul, a piddling note of regret. At one point, he notes his incongruous fondness for the local insects. “Sometimes I feel like I care more about the moths of Chile,” he says, “than I do about the people of Chile.”

Chris regards his role in the deaths and disappearances of thousands of innocents with a weary shrug—and, on rare dark nights of the soul, a piddling note of regret.
At one point, he notes his incongruous fondness for the local insects.
“Sometimes I feel like I care more about the moths of Chile,” he says, “than I do about the people of Chile.”

paragraphs.text: McDonagh grants us a touristic view of Chile masquerading as a geopolitical one, and his dramatic aims are as obvious and limited as his emotional agenda. We’re meant to find Chris pitiable because of his diagnosis, and we’re meant to find him redeemable when he offers sincere advice to the naïvely idealistic Monica, warning her of the forthcoming horrors of the Pinochet regime. The final passages of “Wild Horse Nine” are at once swift and interminable, the action-thriller elements snapping into place at last, only to be hijacked by an exceedingly long goodbye. You can’t accuse McDonagh of not knowing his priorities; we are to shed bountiful tears for Chris, with perhaps a few to spare for his collateral damage. Some of us may be forgiven for resisting the invitation. I remained dry of eye—and rooted for the cancer.

chapters.title: “I Love You in the Morning”

paragraphs.text: Haven’t I slogged through enough regrets? Aren’t my hoovesmud-caked and heavy? I used to think things likeHow could anyone . . . ? and then I found out.What makes up a life?My father escaped the pogroms in Russiaon the shoulders of his mother and an older brother.Hiding in the forest by day, they trudged through snow at night.My father. Who stood hunched behind the counterof Hy-Grade Wines & Liquors, who partedhis hair in the middle and left a grease stain on the couch.Who loved watermelon.Now I’m so much older than he lived to be.Last week I couldn’t remember Stevie Wonder’s name.I could see his big, beautiful head swaying.But it took me all day to haul his name up, hand over hand,from the murky well. That same nightI forgot Hemingway’s first name.Now I go around saying, Ernest Hemingway, Stevie Wonder.Ernest Hemingway, Stevie Wonder.And why then can I still recallmy legions of failures. Lashing out at my childwhen I thought I’d lost her in a strange city.The newborn possums I smashedwith a shovel in the garden shed.And Celia who came to my door the nightshe had nowhere to go. Yes,there were circumstances, butI didn’t take her in. And everyoneI’ve lost or abandoned. What ifI didn’t keep shuffling through the litterof my sins and lamentations.Tonight when I go out to lock up the chickensthe orange dahlias glow, each petaltender and suffused with the last light of day.Beauty. That’s an old story too.I may never get to Paris again, but once I heardGhislaine Roux sing “Ave Maria” at Sainte-Chapelle.Sun streamed through the dazzling stained glass.I was so close I could see the fine mist of sweat on her throat.I was washed in a river of splendor.And yet I’ve been so unhappy.I’ve thrown down a towel to soften the tileon the bathroom floor, lain there and cried, I can’t bear it. Ican’t bear it.And then another voice said, not without pity,Of course you can.And I rinsed my face, opened the door,and smiled at the child coloring at the table.Have I had a good life? Once after sexwhile I lay heavy on the body of my beloved,for a second, two seconds, I could feel it—good and bad collapsinglike a wave breaking into the sea.And then the next second I thought about itand it was the aboutness again.The baby keeps saying, I can’t remember.At two, is she already forgetting everythingshe knew before she was born?Yesterday, she put a piece of paperthe size of her thumbnail into a toy mailbox.Then she took it out and read the letter to me.Dear Nana. I love you in the morning.Then she put it back in the box.Do you want to hear it again? she asked.
